utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning again, Your Honours. Picking up where I left off yesterday on the burden of proof, I do wish to add one point and that is to ask the Trial Chamber to carefully review the Prosecution's final brief and final argument to determine whether they have actually applied the right burden of proof to the arguments they advance. Indeed, at trial, it would occur that the Prosecution would examine witnesses without regard to the proper standard of proof. See, for example, the cross-examination of Professor Corn, transcript 21481, lines 14 to 16. If you turn to page 514 of the Prosecution's final brief, the Prosecution says: "Even Defence expert Corn, who believed it was not Gotovina's intention to shell whole towns, acknowledged that a reasonable interpretation of Gotovina's order is an order to conduct an unlawful attack on those towns. Of course, what the Prosecution has to prove is the inverse. That is, that Professor Corn's interpretation is unreasonable and the Prosecution's interpretation is the only reasonable interpretation of the evidence. We also ask you to check through some of the murder schedules that the Prosecution appended. See, for example, Annex B, page 27, where the Prosecution says the cause of death is unknown but possibly the victim sustained gun-shot wounds. Or see 283, Annex B, page 11, the witness was probably executed by HV policemen. So we ask you to carefully go through the brief because it does not appear on its face that the Prosecution applied the right burden of proof, nor did the Prosecution claim in its brief that it was applying the right burden of proof. In an effort to convince you that you should not believe your own eyes concerning the express orders of General Gotovina and the entire Croatian leadership to prevent and punish crime, the Prosecution provides the following remarkable statement in its final brief which is tremendously insightful in unravelling the essence of the Prosecution's case against General Gotovina. We can show paragraph 15 of the Prosecution's brief: "JCE members were able to issue generic instructions to prevent or stop the looting and burning, secure in the knowledge that such instructions would be ineffectual - thereby intentionally permitting and condoning crimes while simultaneously creating the false impression that they did not intend them." Your Honours, we give you the simple answer. States and armies give orders because they want them followed. Croatia was no different. Croatia had given similar orders during Operation Flash only three months earlier, and as explained in our brief, Croatia was praised by the Secretary-General and the representatives of the international community, including, Witness Galbraith, who, on the 1st of August, told President Tudjman that Croatia's conduct in Western Slavonia "earned him tremendous credit." The Secretary-General praised Croatia for its efforts to protect the human rights of Serbs in Western Slavonia, and you have seen that in our brief. Why therefore Croatia would be "secure in the knowledge that such instructions would be ineffectual when, in fact, 60 days earlier they were effectual is not explained by the Prosecution. However, I am certain that in rebuttal the Prosecution will come up with a creative conspiracy theory to explain that as well. The Gotovina Defence will advance the simple and straightforward explanation of that evidence. The Prosecution desperately tries to crawl out from under the overwhelming weight of the evidence of the efforts of the Croatian authorities, including General Gotovina, to prevent and punish crime by arguing that their orders to stop criminality were fake orders not intended to be implemented. Yet they offer no evidence in support of that radical inference. You have not seen a single Presidential transcript of secret conversations where someone suggests that orders should be issued but not enforced. No witness testified that they ever heard a suggestion even that fake orders be issued for the benefit of the international community. Indeed, the Prosecution offers you nothing in terms of evidence that would allow the Chamber to cast aside express orders in favour of a radical inference. Indeed, as we point out in our brief at paragraph 375, the Blaskic Appeals Chamber expressly rejected the use of unsubstantiated inferences to disregard express evidence in the record. The Prosecution yesterday tried to distinguish the Blaskic precedent on drawing inferences. It cannot. The fact remains and the law remains that you cannot use unsubstantiated inferences to draw an inference to cast away express evidence to the contrary, and that is the case here. Whether the Trial Chamber could draw an adverse inference if there was evidence of that inference in the record is not an issue that arises in this case. Thus, the Prosecution's reliance on Milutinovic is misplaced. In Milutinovic, the Trial Chamber determined that the accused Pavkovic issued phoney orders to adhere to international law on the basis of specific bad acts by that accused that were contrary to the orders he had issued, such as using units in combat against the express orders of his superiors, omitting relevant knowledge of criminal events from his reports, deliberately underreporting murder incidents to his superiors despite having an express obligation to do so. Here, there is no evidence of any such bad acts by General Gotovina, or President Tudjman. In fact, the express evidence in the record can only lead you to the inference that the highest officials in Croatia, including the named members of the alleged JCE, wanted crime to stop and issued orders to make it stop. The internal conversations of the Croatian authorities to which the international community, the media, and any outsiders were not privy demonstrate that the Croatian leadership established a policy to stop all crime and, in fact, issued orders to stop that crime. See, for example, P463, a private conversation between Radic and Tudjman, two named members of the JCE, where they condemn burning as the worst evil. See Prime Minister Valentic comments in a closed session government meeting on the 23rd of August. That's D426, page 21: "Special care has to be provided to the Serb population." You've seen General Gotovina berating his troops on the 6th of August on the Knin meeting video; again, a private meeting. And if we look on the screen, P918, this is the political affairs warning issued within the chain of command telling subordinates -- we can scroll up, please. In that second paragraph, after condemning crime says: "Following the policy of the Supreme Commander, Dr. Franjo Tudjman as well as the instructions of the Defence minister and the political administration of the Defence Ministry of the Republic of Croatia, it is necessary to immediately prevent the following ... the continued torching and destruction of facilities and property ... the killing of livestock; the confiscation of property; and inappropriate conduct toward remaining civilians and prisoners of war ..." How the Prosecution could say you should draw an inference, and not only an inference but that the inference they suggest is the only reasonable inference that you can draw on the evidence, is unexplained by the Prosecution. It is clear that these are the private conversations, private messages being sent within the Croatian government. That is what the policy is. You have absolutely no evidence from the Prosecution whatsoever that would contradict this message, a note from someone saying, Relax on enforcing orders; don't be in a hurry to investigate. With respect to every single important issue in this case, Your Honours, General Gotovina has asked you to take the simple explanation and the Prosecution has done the opposite. Let's take a look at what each party says on the key issues in this case. The first issue I would like to address is paragraphs 121 and 352 of the Prosecution's final brief. The Prosecution in its final brief has, for the first time, added a new allegation of General Gotovina's participation in the alleged JCE. Now it is alleged that one of the four ways General Gotovina participated in the JCE was by ensuring that General Cermak became the primary conduit for the complaints and queries of international officials and that he did so by telling General Forand, on the 8th of August, that all complaints of internationals, including complaints about crimes, were to be referred directly to General Cermak. This was never put to a single witness in the case. That allegation is not in the indictment. It's not in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. It wasn't argued at 98 bis. The Prosecution thus denied the Chamber and the Defence the ability to test that allegation. Nevertheless, it is clear that this theory is factually wrong. We draw the Trial Chamber's attention to Exhibit D297, which is General Forand's agenda of the 6th of August for a meeting with the "military governor" which UNCRO passed to the HV liaison officer, Witness Lukavic. That was two days before Forand met with General Gotovina. We turn your attention to D1667 which are the notes of Tony Banbury, Mr. Akashi's assistant, of a meeting on the 7th of August between General Cermak, General Forand, John Alstrom, and Yasushi Akashi. And if you turn to page 39 at the bottom, it is clear that General Cermak said: "We will arrange a meeting between your human rights people and my headquarters tomorrow. Headquarters Knin will always be open to you ..." And if we turn the page, to General Forand's complaints about freedom of movement, General Cermak said: "If you have any problems, please see me personally." That was one day before General Forand met with General Gotovina. Accordingly, this claim by the Prosecution must fail. It is clear that this argument is advanced at the last minute, because the Prosecution cannot address a fundamental issue raised by the Defence throughout the trial, and that is that no one went to General Gotovina to address crime after Operation Storm. While the Prosecution can easily try to dismiss that with respect to Croatian officials by simply saying they were in a JCE, so, of course, they had secretly decided not to go to the man who could solve all the problems because that was part of the conspiracy. They couldn't address why the internationals weren't going to General Gotovina, so, playing Devil's Advocate, they turned it around and said it must be because General Gotovina did something devious to deflect the internationals in furtherance of the JCE, so the lack of notice to General Gotovina is, in fact, proof of his guilt. Again, that's the conspiracy theory. In paragraph 121 of its brief, the Prosecution argues that a second way that General Gotovina participated in the JCE was by deliberately failing to take necessary and reasonable measures. It should be noted that we called an expert witness, General Jones, a three-star US general with 36 years of experience, to testify specifically about necessary and reasonable measures. That is because the Prosecution, just weeks before the end of the Prosecution case, decided not to call its expert, General Pringle, to testify as to whether he believed General Gotovina took all necessary and reasonable measures under the circumstances. So we called General Jones who testified on direct examination that General Gotovina took all necessary and reasonable measures, before, during and after Operation Storm, and added that he couldn't think of a single thing that he would have done differently in General Gotovina's place. Through this testimony in direct examination, Your Honours, the Gotovina Defence put a challenge directly to the Prosecution, pursuant to Rule 90(H): Put your best case forward as to what the necessary and reasonable measures were that General Gotovina allegedly failed to take. The best case they could put forward can be found in footnotes 1048, 1050, and 1051 of the Gotovina Defence final brief. Because those Prosecution arguments were discredited during trial and during the cross-examination of General Jones, the Prosecution now advances new arguments concerning necessary and reasonable measures that were never advanced at trial. For the record, we object to these new arguments being raised for the first time in final argument and final briefs, denying the Trial Chamber and General Gotovina the opportunity to challenge those theories, to cross-examine witnesses on them, to put its own witnesses on to rebut those claims. The time to advance the arguments the Prosecution is advancing now was when a three-star US general testified that General Gotovina took all necessary and reasonable measures. That was the time to confront General Jones and General Gotovina because then those new theories could be tested. Because the Trial Chamber cannot test the new theories advanced by the Prosecution, they should be afforded no weight. What you should rely on is the expert testimony of General Jones and contrast it with the case the Prosecution put to him in cross-examination. You should not rely on the bald opinions of Prosecution trial counsel on what necessary and reasonable measures would have been. On the issue of effective control, first, Your Honours, let me preface this by saying, in the entire discussion yesterday about necessary and reasonable measures, effective control, notice, you were again never told what the burden of proof is and never told whether the analysis you were being put forward -- or that was being put forward was being measured against the burden of proof. As the Chamber is aware, the Appeals Chamber has ruled that with respect to each element of command responsibility the Prosecution must prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt. That means you must conclude that there is no reasonable interpretation of the evidence other than that General Gotovina had effective control, other than that he had notice, and other than that he failed to take necessary and reasonable measures. Now with respect to the issue of effective control, the Trial Chamber specifically asked the Prosecution to address the commentary to Article 87 of the protocol of the Geneva Conventions. That provision says it is self-evident that the obligation applies in the context of the responsibilities as they have devolved over different levels of the hierarchy, and that the duties of the non-commissioned officer are not identical to those of a battalion commander, and the duties of the latter are not identical to those of the divisional commander. Now, despite the Trial Chamber specifically asking the Prosecution to address this issue, in essence you were told yesterday the commentary is irrelevant. You were never told what in the context of this case it means that the obligation applies as the responsibilities devolve over different levels of the hierarchy. The Prosecution remains of the view that General Gotovina, at the top of the chain of command, should have taken the measures that an NCO at the bottom of the chain of command would take. Moreover, we dispute the Prosecution's claim that we have somehow misstated the Oric Appeals Chamber decision. We quoted it verbatim in a block quote in our brief. The Prosecution left out this portion of the Appeals Chamber's finding: "The separate question of whether - due to proximity or remoteness of control - the superior indeed possessed effective control is a matter of evidence, not of substantive law." That is at paragraph 618 of our brief. That is the issue we raised. The Prosecution doesn't respond. With respect to the issue of Grahovo, General Jones testified that prior to Storm, General Gotovina took all necessary and reasonable measures after the Grahovo operation to prevent and punish crime. The Prosecution offered no expert testimony to contradict General Jones's opinion. Moreover, the Prosecution ignores the context in which General Gotovina was operating after the Grahovo operation but prior to Operation Storm. For example, Prosecution completely ignores Operation Vaganj and the fact that the Croatian leadership was aware that the Serbs were planning an attack by forces under Ratko Mladic's command against General Gotovina's forces in the Grahovo-Glamoc area. Which turned out to be true, because the VRS Drina Corps arrived in the Grahovo area on the 9th of August. It is within that context, General Gotovina facing an imminent threat, that he was forced to take the measures that were reasonable in those circumstances. The Prosecution falsely claims, at paragraph 151 and again in its argument yesterday, that: "General Gotovina took steps to conceal his subordinates' crimes at Grahovo" by ordering that "report through a messenger that Glamoc and Grahovo were shelled by phosphoric shells." The Prosecution, of course, ignores the fact that what General Gotovina said was the truth. In fact, the wider areas of Grahovo and Glamoc, i.e., the forested areas, were shelled by phosphoric shells by the HV. That's Exhibit D1980. And indeed, Ratko Mladic in his diary, on the 2nd of August, referenced incendiary munitions. That's D1465, e-court page 243. Accordingly, the Prosecution condemns General Gotovina for reporting the truth. Next the Prosecution argues that General Gotovina somehow is responsible because troops under his command had suffered in the four and a half prior years at the hands of the Serbian JCE and that, therefore, they were prone to revenge. Your Honours, virtually everyone in Croatia had suffered some injustice during the war in Croatia. From Vukovar and Ilok in the east, all the way to Dubrovnik and Prevlaka in the far south. In theory, virtually every Croatian could have had a motive for revenge. The Prosecution argues that it does not dispute Croatia's right to retake its lands, it just disputes Croatia's right to use Croatians to do it. On the issue of necessary and reasonable measures, we have said all along that General Gotovina took necessary and reasonable measures to prevent and punish crime. Look at the evidence, Your Honours. General Gotovina was there when Minister Susak passed on the US conditions, on the 2nd of August, to the entire military leadership. Again, a private conversation, a state-secret conversation. Which included that Military District commanders were to pass on orders to prevent "any kind of uncontrolled conduct, torching, looting, et cetera." That's Exhibit D409. As Lausic testified, Susak also ordered that measures be taken to prevent any behaviour that would require soldiers to be brought before a court. That's transcript 15166, lines 14 to 22. Yet OTP says, at paragraph 16 of its brief, that Susak's order which was given in private to the top officials of the military was essentially a pretend order "aimed at avoiding liability for the crimes rather than genuinely preventing them." The Prosecution, of course, fails to identify who Susak was allegedly pretending to. Nor is there any evidence in the record, in the form of witness testimony, Presidential transcript and the like, to support OTP's inference that Minister Susak's order was not intended to be followed. Again, Your Honours, the Gotovina Defence says that when Minister Susak order that "any kind of uncontrolled conduct," including torching and looting were to be prevented, that's what he meant. The Prosecution says when Susak privately told the military leadership to prevent looting and torching he meant allow looting and torching. General Gotovina issued explicit orders prior to Storm that all criminal activity was to be eliminated. Consistent with the US conditions and Susak's instructions, General Gotovina issued the order at Exhibit D201, page 2. Here's what he ordered: "Familiarising units with the need to eliminate all negative occurrences that will surface in the course of combat operations with a focus on preventing torching and destruction of larger populated areas and towns." Now, even though General Gotovina ordered the elimination of all negative occurrences, the Prosecution argues that this order meant that units should protect populated areas but that General Gotovina wanted them to burn down rural areas. If we could see paragraphs 156 and 157 of the Prosecution's final brief. The second sentence there: "The Political Activities Plan attachment indicates that Gotovina and the Split MD Command expected burning and destruction to occur and accepted the anticipated destruction of rural areas. "Consistent with those instructions and with the JCE members' focus on quickly colonising the larger towns in the Krajina with Croats, Croatian forces left the larger towns relatively intact, but devastated rural areas in Sector South." Herein lies another fundamental contradiction in the Prosecution's case. The Prosecution doesn't argue that General Gotovina was issuing weak, repetitive, ineffective orders. They do that later when they try to discredit General Gotovina. They're arguing here that General Gotovina issued an effective order, that General Gotovina issued an order to protect the larger towns and that that order was implemented, but that General Gotovina deliberately failed to mention rural areas, thereby signalling to subordinates that he wanted them burned down. Again, the Prosecution is alleging that General Gotovina issued effective orders prior to Storm. I ask you, Your Honours, is this interpretation by the Prosecution the only reasonable interpretation of this order? This is nonsense. We say that when General Gotovina ordered the elimination of all negative occurrences he meant eliminate all negative occurrences. The Prosecution argues that it means, I order you to burn down rural areas. Once again, they never put this interpretation of this order to anyone, nor is there any evidence in the record to support their interpretation. Not even Theunens suggested. But in their blind zeal to obtain a conviction, the Prosecution would rather argue the ridiculous than concede an obvious point. Further on in D201, at page 2, General Gotovina orders advising members of units on conduct with civilians and POWs in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. Now, what the Prosecution claims is a boiler-plate order, in fact, was put into practice. At paragraph 125 the Prosecution calls it a generic reference to the Geneva Convention that was "manifestly inadequate." Apparently General Gotovina, according to the Prosecution, should have itemised what Croatian forces shouldn't do: Don't kill, don't burn, don't loot, don't torture. They never put this claim to any witness. But you heard that this order was implemented. You heard that booklets were handed out on the Geneva Conventions to troops prior to Storm. Those booklets are in evidence as D533 and D1602. As Witness Sudac testified at transcript 21367, lines 21 to 24, the commanders did, in fact, itemise for their subordinates what General Gotovina wanted: "I remember what our superior officers were telling us. It was a war and we remembered the most important things. Don't kill, don't loot, don't rape, help all those who are wounded, such basic things." Evidently, Your Honours, General Gotovina's subordinate commanders were able to figure out just fine what General Gotovina wanted when he ordered that units must treat civilians and POWs in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. You saw that subordinate commanders, such as the commander of the 4th Guards Brigade, passed down these orders to their subordinates. That's P1202, page 12. During Operation Storm, General Gotovina continued to place an emphasis on preventing crime. On the evening of 4 August, the political affairs officer, at the evening briefing, reminded all commanders that Knin must not suffer the same fate as Grahovo. On the morning of 5 August, General Gotovina personally ordered "maximum fairness towards civilians and the UN," in all operative groups and -- and to all commanders as his forces were about to enter populated areas, such as Knin. On 6 August, you have seen the Knin video many times, where General Gotovina demanded proper conduct by subordinates. Once again, the Prosecution contradicts itself on this video. First it claims, in paragraph 166, towards the bottom, as Cermak observed, Gotovina was "not upset about the crimes and what the military had done, he was upset because the town was dirty and there were no state signs anywhere." But when they had to write a section on General Cermak, at paragraph 358, apparently the person who wrote the Cermak portion of brief didn't coordinate the portion with the Gotovina portion of the brief so we get this admission: "Cermak attended Gotovina's briefing in Knin Fortress on 6 August 1995, from where villages around Knin were plainly seen burning, and heard Gotovina berate HV commanders for the looting and misdeeds of HV soldiers." Well, which one is it? Was he berating HV commanders for the looting and misdeeds of HV soldiers, as is plainly evident on the video? Or did he not care about that and just was concerned that the town was dirty. Your Honours, no reasonable person could look at that video and say that General Gotovina did not have a genuine intent to prevent and punish crime. On the 10th of August, General Gotovina issued D204. If we can see this on Sanction, please. On its face, in the subject line it says: "Order on compliance with military disciplinary measures." In point 1 -- actually in the introduction, it says it is being issued in order to prevent theft of property, undisciplined conduct, and to save human lives. Contrary to the Prosecution's claim that General Gotovina issued this order pursuant to an order from General Cervenko, you will see that nothing in the introduction indicates as such. And you've seen many orders where the Court can confirm the standard procedure was to refer to a superior order if, in fact, someone was acting pursuant to it. In point 1, General Gotovina prohibits arbitrary movement of HV members in the liberated areas without the knowledge of superior commanders. If we go to paragraph 2, he says: "Take all necessary measures and fully engage in the implementation of the military disciplinary conduct and the maintenance of order in the area of responsibility, and prevent arson and all other illegal acts. Take resolute measures against anybody who conducts himself in an undisciplined manner." You have seen P918, which we saw earlier this morning. It specifically not only says what the policy is, what the policy of President Tudjman and Minister Susak is, but if we scroll to the bottom of the page please, in bold: "In cooperation with the information and security service," that would be the SIS, "and the military police, take repressive measures and launch disciplinary proceedings [sic] against those who do not abide by the instructions." Despite this, the Prosecution at paragraph 221 of its brief says: "Gotovina did not consider his subordinates' crimes against Serbs and their property to constitute a problem of military discipline." At paragraph 223 they say: "Gotovina's orders contain no explicit instructions to his subordinates to impose disciplinary measures to address indictment crimes." Well, Your Honours, the only way anyone could conclude that is if you choose to ignore D204 and P918. Is this the only reasonable explanation of the evidence which is the Prosecution's burden of proof? Moreover, they never put this interpretation to General Jones when they had a Rule 90(H) obligation to do so. With respect to demobilisation, Your Honours, it is absolutely clear that General Lausic testified that the most effective disciplinary measure available was demobilisation. P2159, paragraphs 191 and 211. Moreover, Witnesses Botteri concurred. The Prosecution mischaracterises General Lausic's position. And if we turn to the next exhibit, this is also from P2159, paragraphs 35 and 36, from the statement of Mate Lausic. And he explains not only the use of demobilisation but what the role of the SIS is, and this is instructive to address the Prosecution's arguments yesterday about who had command over political affairs and SIS. Read carefully how Mr. Lausic explained the role of political affairs, SIS and the military police. And he says it was the role of SIS to observe and then to report a problem to a commander, and to eliminate any person from the unit who was likely to be a problem. Beginning of page 36: "For example, a SIS officer tells a battalion commander there was a member who should be demobilised. Let's say the commander says, 'All right leave him here, he is okay.' This SIS officer's commander would be told at SIS centre." And then if you read the rest of the paragraph, SIS goes all the way to Zagreb and up the military chain of command, if necessary. But this goes back to all of the litigation we had about vertical subordination and horizontal coordination with the Split Military District Command. The Prosecution, nevertheless, insists that demobilisation "was an attempt by Gotovina and his subordinate commanders to absolve themselves of responsibility for criminal elements within the HV." There is, of course -- and this is at paragraph 231. There's, of course, a glaring absence of a footnote in the Prosecution's brief for that proposition. Why? Because they're making it up. There's no evidence in the record to support that position. No one testified to it. They did not put this position to -- proposition to any witness in the case, not to Lausic himself, not to General Jones, not even to Theunens. Indeed, what you are offered on the issue of demobilisation is the opinion of Prosecution trial counsel. That is not proper evidence for this Trial Chamber to consider. In fact, the only evidence in the record is from the Prosecution's own witnesses, Lausic and Botteri, that demobilisation was the most effective disciplinary measure under the circumstances. The Prosecution also claims in its brief that there is no evidence of a single demobilised soldier subsequently being prosecuted for a crime. That's at paragraph 233. This is false. See, for example, several examples contained within Exhibit D1381. Moreover, Witness Perkovic was a viva voce Defence witness who testified that he was demobilised while in custody as a result of his alleged involvement in the Varivode murders and subsequently was prosecuted for those murders. That's transcript 19527, lines 12 to 21; 19546, line 23, to 19547, line 7. The Prosecution claims at paragraph 155 of their brief and argued again yesterday that General Gotovina ordered no reporting or monitoring of his orders to prevent and punish crime. You were told yesterday General Gotovina "expected his orders to fail and when they did not -- and when they did, he did not want to know about it." In fact, as the Prosecution is very well aware and which they implicitly admitted at the end of their argument yesterday, General Gotovina didn't have to issue a separate order to report on the implementation of these orders because that was already the job of political affairs and SIS. And in fact, they did report back to General Gotovina on the implementation of those orders and we have those reports in evidence; D984, D810, P1133, P1134. Now, after first arguing that General Gotovina ordered no reporting, the Prosecution later tried to say that the political affairs was subordinated to General Gotovina and that part of the job of the political affairs officer of the Split Military District staff was "monitoring." Well, monitoring what? Monitoring the implementation of General Gotovina 's orders. Prosecution can't have it both ways, and the evidence, including the documentary evidence I just cited, is perfectly clear that there was monitoring of the implementation of General Gotovina's orders. We also saw, at nightly briefings, that MPs would advise if there was a problem in the chain of command. That's P71, page 116. We also saw commanders reporting problems at the nightly briefings. P71 again, page 116. And we saw that every single time that a problem was reported back to General Gotovina, General Gotovina took action. The Prosecution cannot keep its story straight as to whether General Gotovina was issuing effective orders or ineffective orders. The Prosecution's positions depend solely on the context, whether General Gotovina would in the context be more discredited by saying that his orders were effective or by saying his orders were ineffective. For example, the Prosecution's argument rests on arguing that General Gotovina's artillery order was effective. His orders to protect the UN were effective. That's paragraph 17. His orders to not hit the UNCRO camp were effective. And as I just showed you a few moments ago, at paragraphs 156 and 157, they argue that General Gotovina's orders to protect populated areas from burning were effective. Now, then, however, at paragraph 192, they argue that General Gotovina's repeated orders encouraged the commission of crimes. They can't deal with the fact that General Gotovina was issuing orders to stop crime so they try to dismiss by saying it was ineffective after starting from the premise that it was General Gotovina's effective order to protect larger towns from burning. Why General Gotovina would think that his orders to protect larger towns would be effective but would think that his orders to protect rural areas from burning, to stop looting, to take disciplinary action, would be ineffective, is, of course, completely unexplained by the Prosecution. There is no logic to what they argue. Moreover, as the Prosecution explained to you how a subordinate would know which are the orders that are supposed to be followed and which are the orders that are supposed to be ignored. Again, how is it that subordinates were able to figure out General Gotovina's intention to protect larger towns but weren't able to figure out or implement his intention to stop crime everywhere else? We turn to paragraph 164 of the Prosecution's brief. "Although Gotovina" -- this is in the middle of the paragraph: "Although Gotovina issued orders that acknowledged these crimes and contained - at least on their face - measures to prevent their continued commission, the content, timing, and number of these orders reveal that Gotovina was pretending to address these crimes while allowing and encouraging their continuance." Pretending to whom, Your Honours? Pretending to his subordinates? This is -- General Gotovina is issuing internal classified orders. He is not issuing orders to the international press. Pretending to whom, I ask the Prosecution. This argument is truly ridiculous, let alone the only reasonable explanation of the evidence. Moreover, once again, they failed to put this argument to any witness in the case. Not to General Jones, not even to Mr. Theunens. The Prosecution argues that by issuing multiple orders to stop crime, "it is only logical" that Gotovina was encouraging crime. Again, no footnote. You'll have to determine, Your Honours, whether the Prosecution's logic is logic you're willing to adopt as the only reasonable interpretation of the evidence. At paragraph 718 of our -- turning now to the attention -- to the question of what the Prosecution claims are measures General Gotovina could have taken, at paragraph 718 of our brief, we explain that the test is necessary measures are appropriate measures which show that the superior genuinely tried to prevent or punish; and reasonable measures are those reasonably falling within the material powers of the superior. Now, the steps that -- most of the steps that the Prosecution identifies in its brief were never put to anyone. According to the Prosecution yesterday, these were "simple and obvious steps." Yet the Prosecution, for some reason, never put most of these simple and obvious steps to any witness in two and a half years of trial. What you heard yesterday in respect to measures within -- against the 134th Home Guard units was based on the military expertise of no one. They are the opinions of Prosecution trial counsel not to put to any witness in the case. They are arguments made up out of whole cloth. Your Honours, when comparing the Defence arguments and the Prosecution arguments, we ask you to note that we called an expert witness who testified that he would have chosen General Gotovina's steps and necessary and reasonable measures. With respect to the measures suggested by the Prosecution yesterday, no one testified that they would have taken those steps. Nevertheless, most of the steps that the Prosecution suggested were in fact implemented. As mentioned previously General Gotovina did not have to issue a separate order on -- on reporting of implementation. General Gotovina did issue orders to enforce disciplinary measures; that's D204 and P918. The Prosecution says that General Gotovina should have tasked the MPs to control crime. This issue has been litigated extensively and doesn't require any further comment, other than to stay that we are confident that the Trial Chamber has well understood who was in command of deploying the military police for crime prevention, investigation, and prosecution. Moreover, I must point out that in discussing the military police, the Prosecution repeatedly claims, such as in paragraph 238, that General Gotovina exercised "command and control over the military police." There is absolutely no evidence for that claim in the evidence. Article 8 makes clear that command and control rested with Lausic alone. It is evident that the Prosecution still does not grasp the concepts of command and control and that command is not synonymous with control. Mr. President, you tried to alert the parties to this distinction, at transcript 2395, lines 8 to 19. And General Forand tried to explain it to the parties, at transcript 4343, line 22, to 4344, line 4. Unfortunately, the Prosecution still does not understand. The Prosecution argues that General Gotovina should have imposed military curfews in Croatia. This argument plainly ignores Croatian law and essentially argues that General Gotovina should have enacted a military coup d'etat against the civilian government of Croatia. It is clear that General Gotovina did not have the legal power to declare a military curfew in liberated areas when the constitutional order of Croatia had been restored. Clearly, the Prosecution would rather advance another hopelessly unsubstantiated argument rather than concede the obvious. Finally, the Prosecution claims that General Gotovina should have removed or replaced commanders or imposed disciplinary measures against commanders. This was never mentioned before their final brief. Which commanders, Your Honours? For what? Well, we don't know. And the Trial Chamber doesn't know. Because the Prosecution failed to put this theory to anyone. Not to Theunens, not to General Jones. The Prosecution, of course, will now likely say that he should have disciplined every commander or replaced every commander. Unfortunately, we cannot respond to any such allegation because it hasn't been raised before. Now consider this: You are being asked to find that General Gotovina failed -- his failure to take such obvious measures was so clear, was so blatantly self-evident that you should find not only that General Gotovina bears responsibility under 7(3), but that it went a step further to wilful intent to allow burning and looting. Yet these obvious self-evident steps were never raised in two and a half years of trial. I think that speaks for itself, Your Honours. We met the case the Prosecution put forward at trial. The rest of these new arguments no weight and no citation to the record. You must conclude that General Jones's opinion is a reasonable interpretation of the evidence. Finally, the Prosecution completely ignores a fundamental issue in our brief, a fundamental issue we raised in opening statement, a fundamental issue we raised with countless witnesses in this case. It is ignored in their final brief and ignored yesterday. Why is it that no one went to General Gotovina after the 6th of August to ask him to do anything? How can it be that General Gotovina is in command of the military police that Lausic is coordinating with the Ministry of the Interior on actions to be taken and yet Lausic never once communicates with General Gotovina? How can it be that Moric testified that General Gotovina's name never came up in conversations on this issue, or that the president's office never discussed General Gotovina on this issue? Or that General Forand writes a letter, one letter, to General Gotovina after Operation Storm to complain about UNCRO vehicles, to complain about treatment of UNCRO at check-points, and to ask General Gotovina to help him write his analysis of Operation Storm for the Canadian government? Never wrote him a letter or even included within that letter a claim that, General Gotovina, your forces are engaged in widespread systematic burning and looting, and you must get them under control. It is completely unaddressed. Your Honours, there was a point at this trial where the Trial Chamber said to General Cross, you would expect that if you are going to be involved in implementation, you should be involved in the planning. I submit to you that that is a blatantly obvious point that the Defence accepts but the Prosecution does not. I take it a step further, Your Honours. It is a blatantly obvious point that if you are involved in the execution, you would expect that you would be contacted to address the matter. General Gotovina was not. In fact, we saw that General Cervenko, General Gotovina's superior, was prepared to directly address General Gotovina whenever he had a concern about General Gotovina. As we see in the alleged mistreatment of Alun Roberts, General Cervenko demanded an explanation from General Gotovina and got it. General Cervenko never once contacted General Gotovina to say, You are not complying with your obligations to enforce discipline. Your Honours, let me conclude by saying that it is absolutely abundantly clear that General Gotovina took all necessary and reasonable measures under the circumstances, and you must enter a judgement of acquittal. I will now turn over the floor to Mr. Kehoe, who will address issues of the crime base, artillery, and other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm looking at the clock. May I take it that you prefer to -- will you take all the remaining 90 minutes or will there be any further division of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There will be a further division. There is some concluding comments of approximately 30 minutes by my colleague Mr. Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I leave it to some extent to you where to take the break if it is stays within the usual limits. Please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I will. And I trust that the Chamber will want to break at the usual time of approximately 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if, for example, if ten minutes later you would be finished and someone else would take over, then we would, of course, take the break ten minutes later. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly. Your Honours, Court staff, my learned colleagues on both sides of the well, good morning. Before I go into the comments that I have on various aspects of this, I want to harken back just initially to the comments made my friends across the well on the need for accuracy and the need for the Court to carefully examine citations in these briefs, and I know the Chamber will do so, and I know the Chamber will purposely and directly examine many of the allegations, some very serious allegations levelled against these three accused. And I know when the Prosecution levels charges that in the use of artillery in Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac, that use of artillery caused civilian deaths and injuries, and I know the Chamber will look and examine that evidence of civilian deaths and injuries in Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac which the Prosecution mentions in paragraphs 138, 484, and will examine that evidence to see what those deaths and injuries were. Unfortunately, the Chamber will look in vain, because when leveling those allegations against the accused and most particularly against General Gotovina, there is no evidence of any civilian deaths, injuries in Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac. So what we learn from the brief that is filed by the Prosecution, that merely because it is said, one need to check the accuracy of that. And it is not only what is said that needs to be questioned when it comes from the Prosecution but what is not said. Unfortunately, silence is often sacrificed in the pursuit of the truth. And when in alleging that virtually the entire political, civil and military structure of Croatia was involved in the joint criminal enterprise to ensure that the Serb population was not allowed to come back to Croatia, never once in a 300-page brief, never once in six hours of argument, never once does the Prosecution comment about the prosecutor Mr. Galovic who testified to this Chamber, in February of 1996 -- that he had processed 1277 cases in the wake of Operation Storm by February of 1996. The question to be asked by the Chamber is why. Why would the Prosecution fail to mention that? Is he, as termed in their brief at paragraph 5, just simply one of the many JCE members who are too numerous to mention? Or was there some reason that these inaccuracies and these omissions are merely sacrifices on the altar of a conviction? I turn my attention to the allegations concerning General Gotovina as it pertains to the JCE, and I direct the Chamber to the factors set forth by the Prosecution in paragraph 121 of its brief. Factor 1 of paragraph 121 is that General Gotovina shared the common criminal purpose of the JCE by allegedly planning, ordering and implementing a widespread and systematic unlawful shelling attack against the Serb civilian population with the specific purpose of driving that population out. These comments were -- will be addressed in part to the filed by the Prosecution and also to the comments presented by Mr. Russo yesterday. This use of artillery is the core of the Prosecution's Brioni JCE theory which depends upon proof of widespread or systematic unlawful shelling. While a centre-piece of the Prosecutor's JCE theory, there is simply no evidence to support that theory. The evidence demonstrates that the HV's use of artillery during Operation Storm was consistent with widely accepted military doctrine, not only on the NATO level, not only on the Dutch army level, not only on the American level, but throughout militaries in the world. And this is precisely what the Gotovina Defence told the Chamber during our opening statement, which is at page 573, lines 6 through 24. Well, this is extensively covered in our brief at pages 50 through 86, Your Honours, and I will not obviously go through that, taking the admonition from the Chamber not to re-argue that which is in our brief. I must comment on some of the arguments that were brought before this Chamber by Mr. Russo yesterday. My page references to the transcript yesterday, Mr. President and Your Honours, are to the raw copy, simply because there was no final copy available last night while this preparation was underway, so my apologies in that regard. At page 47 of yesterday's transcript, line 24 through 48 -- excuse me, line 24 through -- page 48, line 3, Mr. Russo argued: "No amount of artillery jargon about the centre of gravity or full-spectrum operational dominance or air/land battle or the manoeuvrist approach or other any other military doctrine justifies the wild discrepancies between the alleged targets of attack and the actual evidence of what was shelled in Knin." Now first and foremost, Mr. Russo at no point in the brief or yesterday attempts to discuss any of those accepted military approaches because they are just that, accepted military approaches that are counter to the position taken by the Prosecution. Next, Mr. Russo then showed the Chamber a slide overlaying circles of where witnesses claimed to have seen shells or rockets land at some point during Storm along with 11 military targets identified by Mr. Rajcic. Now if we could put this on Sanction for a moment. This is the slide that was referred to yesterday by Mr. Russo. Now the Prosecution asked the Chamber to infer from this slide that the only reasonable interpretation of the evidence is that the entire city of Knin was made the object of attack. This slide is not only not probative of that point, it isn't probative of virtual nothing. In looking at this, and consistent with what the Chamber has done in cases like Galovic, the questions are manyfold. The first question is whether the recollection of witnesses, in the midst of this combat, as to where shells allegedly landed was accurate and, in fact, landed in these various areas circled in the map of Knin. The next question, of course, would be, if the circles of these witnesses were correct, the Chamber would need to know the concentration of fire of impacts within these circles for it to be probative of anything. How many -- how many shells fell on these circles? One? 50? 100? Further, the Chamber would need to know, within these circles, where the shells impacted relative to military targets. These questions could have and should have been answered, as it was in all the cases such as Galovic, by evidence of damage within these circles; crater analysis, damage assessments, videos, photographs. All of those pieces of evidence presented to other Trial Chambers in support of an illegal shelling charge, none of which has been presented here. Based on Prosecution's slide and its statement yesterday that no less than a thousand artillery shells were fired into Knin over the course of a 25-hour artillery campaign - and again that is page 48 of yesterday's transcript, lines 13 to 14 - the Chamber would have expected to been presented with photographs, videos and damage -- damage assessments in the city of Knin, and that Knin had had been virtually levelled, as a result of this artillery attack. Further, the Chamber would have expected to have received dozens of crater analyses, as well as a disproportionate number of civilian casualties and deaths. The Chamber would not, would not have expected to see evidence that the artillery use was concentrated against military objectives, as outlined by my colleague Mr. Misetic, as we saw in the provisional and final assessment of damage caused by artillery use by senior UNMO Steinar Hjertnes, the report of UN CIVPOL, the reports of senior international diplomats, US code cables, and a US Secretary-General report to the Security Council. This evidence is detailed at paragraphs 306 to 313 in our brief. Additionally, Your Honours, and this was before it was manipulated by Mr. Roberts, the Chamber would not have expected to see General Forand tell the Canadian military, in June of 1996, that the HV's use of artillery was excellent. And that's at P401, page 21. All of the evidence is consistent with the conclusion that the use of artillery was lawful. The fact that the Prosecution did not corroborate widespread -- any widespread destruction in Knin with photographs, videos, damage assessments, crater analysis, and disproportionate civilian casualties is not just because they waited three months into trial to file a motion seeking artillery documents from Croatia. If this -- Prosecution's interpretation was correct, this type of evidence would have been easily obtainable by the UN and given to the OTP back in 1995. It was not. The reason why it wasn't given to the OTP back in 1995 is because it didn't exist and this after-the-fact interpretation by the Prosecution is simply wrong. To the question, possible question, that the OTP did not have the opportunity to investigate this in August of 1995, I address the Chamber to P378, which is a -- an UNMO report. The OTP has been investigating this case since 29 August 1995, when Mr. Todd Cleaver of the Office of the Prosecutor went -- visited Knin to meet with various UN personnel. Had this evidence existed of this widespread, unlawful attack against the civilian population in Knin, it is simply implausible that that evidence would not have been given to Mr. Cleaver at that time. With respect to crater analysis and the lack thereof, the Prosecution has offered only one evidence -- one crater analysis throughout this entire case. As discussed in paragraph 318 of our brief, this analysis was shown to have been from a Serbian rocket fired into Knin on 5 August. I'm sure Your Honours recall that testimony coming from Mr. Munkelien and Mr. Anttila, as well as their report which showed that this rocket was found in three separate locations, but, nevertheless, the rocket itself was a Serb rocket, an ARSK rocket. Rather than accept this reasonable interpretation of the evidence, in the Prosecution's zeal, the Prosecution now claims - and I kid you not that this is in fact the position that they take - the Prosecution now claims in paragraph 605 of its brief that HV forces seized MRLs at 8.55 from the ARSK and then decided to fire on their own troops who entered Knin by 10.00 on the 5th of August. This -- this is another example of just wide, vacuous speculation on behalf of the Prosecution. There is no evidence to substantiate that allegation at all. Next, during Mr. Russo's presentation he sweepingly dismissed accepted military doctrine as jargon and failed to apply the doctrine into evidence. This is because in our brief at paragraphs 235 into 250, we established that the use of artillery during Operation Storm was consistent with accepted military doctrine. One example of how the Prosecutor dismissal of the military doctrine leads to an erroneous conclusion is the argument that is made by the Prosecution that General Gotovina somehow deviated from the HV staff directive on 26th June of 1995, following the Brioni meeting on the 31st of July. Our brief discusses this at paragraphs 189 to 235. The position of the Prosecution demonstrates a serious misapprehension of the chain of command at a strategic operational and tactical level. The Prosecution's argument is based on the fact that there are additional targets and names of towns in General Gotovina's attack order. Well, of course, there would be. When the Main Staff issues an order, they do so at a strategic level. When it goes down to the operational level, at the General Gotovina level, an additional targeting takes place. Those -- that targeting focuses on strategic targets as outlined by the HV staff and then the operational targets as developed by a Military District commander and his subordinates in the field. As they move down, of course, there are additional targets as we move from -- through these three levels. The targets discussed by Mr. Rajcic during his testimony, be they in Knin or any other towns discussed, were at the operational level. In addition, as I mentioned, to the strategic and operational targets, the subordinate HV units, in responding to matters during the course of the trial, had tactical targets that they were able to engage as the circumstances developed during battle. A simple proposition as the battle unfolds that targets develop over time. The Gotovina Defence previously presented this issue to the Chamber through D1459 and D1460, where we took the Jagoda chart, for instance, and overlay it on Benkovac to show the targeting of not only the operational targets but the any number of tactical targets in and around Benkovac. And in the interests of time, I just offer that -- the Trial Chamber those cites to explain how the development will transpire from the strategic to the operational to the tactical level. None of the slides shown to you by Mr. Russo relating to the shelling in Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac account for tactical targets at all. In addition to the misunderstanding of military doctrine, the Prosecution misunderstands the significance of documents in the effort to support their argument. For instance, Mr. Russo relied on P2338, which is a coded infantry map, to support its argument, in paragraphs 594 to 605 of its brief, that MRLs were directed against civilian areas. They overlooked the explanation by Mr. Rajcic who directly refuted this position at page 16554, lines 11 through 18, where he explained -- I also have additional cites on that. It is 16554, lines 8, to 16556, line 9. He explained that P338 was a coded infantry map used for communications and general reference points. He always said and testified that to know the precise target you would need the X, Y, Z coordinates which the HV had for every target fired on, as Rajcic confirmed in D1425, paragraph 29, and his testimony at 17641, lines 17 through 22. As you saw in the visual aid presented by Mr. Russo, and if we could turn this ... yeah. S-15 and S-54 coordinate with operational targets identified by Mr. Rajcic. They are also, as Mr. Rajcic would explain, general reference points. Further, S-16, the one of direct interest to the Prosecution, is oriented in line with the northern barracks, another operational target identified by Mr. Rajcic and hit by the HV. In paragraph 601 of its brief, the Prosecution attempts to corroborate their interpretation of P2338 by asserting that Mr. Hill found a rocket at General Forand's residence, which he located being inside S-16. This can be viewed by the next slide presented by Mr. Russo and this an overlay of S-16 with the identification by Hill of Forand's residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No problem, Mr. President. If we can go back to the other chart, in an attempt to support their position, they note that Mr. Hill allegedly found a rocket in this area, in the area which he identified where General Forand lived. Now the first thing we know about this is the rocket identified by Mr. Hill, at 3755, lines 8 to 9 didn't, match the specifications of any HV rocket in use during Operation Storm. Second, what the Prosecution doesn't show you is that Mr. Hill was incorrect about the location of General Forand's residence. Now, Mr. Hill testified before General Forand. This map was never shown to General Forand to accurately assess, did he, in fact, live at that location. The subject, however, did come up with Mr. Dawes. On page 5 and 6 of his witness statement, P980, Mr. Dawes testified that in his second trip into Knin he went in a residential neighbourhood by Forand's residence. You will see from the next slide, which is P586, that -- excuse me, D856, my apologies, from D856, that the area identified by Mr. Dawes as the location of General Forand's residence is different than the one offered by Mr. Hill. Further, as I noted, Prosecution witness Boucher did live in the area of S-16, which can be seen in Exhibit P1179, and although Mr. Boucher testified to artillery fire coming into that area, in the direction towards the northern barracks, as I noted, he mentioned nothing about the MRLs. Finally, the Defence notes that P2338 contains dozens and dozens of circles. Why? Because this is a map that is used for communications and general reference points by infantry. If the Prosecution's position is correct, we submit to you that these circles and artillery fire into all of these circles would have been mentioned in any number of other diaries at an operation and certainly at a tactical level. They were not. Mr. President, I note it's 10.30. I'm about to go into another aspect of this, but it is going to take a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'm addressing the Prosecution, both in the opening statement and yesterday, the Prosecution has drawn our attention to the -- to a false report, at least claimed to be false, about the use of phosphoric bombs in Grahovo. Now that seems to be a factual matter which is strongly opposed by the Defence. The Chamber would be assisted if the Prosecution could point to the evidence that it was a false report, which, I take it, will be based on evidence that no phosphoric shells were used on the attack on Grahovo. If that -- somewhere during these days, if you could clarify that. I may have missed it in the briefs, but that specific issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll address the issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kehoe, are you ready it proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just continuing on and completing these allegations levied by the Prosecution concerning the artillery attack. We know on an examination of Knin there was virtually no damage to civilian structures, and we know that in their allegations concerning Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac, they have presented no evidence of civilian injuries or deaths. Question this horrific attack allegedly put forth by the HV on the 4th. Certainly it caused significant civilian deaths and injuries in Knin. An examination of the evidence, once again, reflects that that is not the case. They have evidence of some people seeing some individuals in a hospital, without any determination as to how those people were killed. But they give us in footnote 1959, the identification of several people they maintain were killed during this attack, briefly referring, through this group, and I refer to clarification schedule 185 through 190, number 205 and 225, when we look at that evidence, the number is narrowed down still further. Number -- victim 225. Testified by Ms. Grubor, who saw this person on the 5th coming into the hospital in Knin. No idea where this person was killed -- was -- was hurt, no idea if it was in military targets, no idea if it was in a combat area, none whatsoever. Yet they offer that as part of their unlawful attack against the civilian population charge. How about the six individuals named in 185 through 190. These are the individuals that were allegedly killed in -- outside the UN barracks on the morning of the 5th of August. What they don't tell you was that at least one of those people was dead already. Nevertheless, he is included in this victim of illegal attack on the civilian population by artillery and MRLs. However, under the best of circumstances, these individuals were killed in a mortar attack. Had nothing to do with long-range artillery, had nothing to do with MRLs. Furthermore, the evidence reflects, as detailed in our brief at paragraph 997, that the people involved didn't know whether or not these people were killed by the ARSK or that mortar was shot by the HV. And if we recall, the evidence in the record was likewise, that prior to that the ARSK did, in fact, target the UN Sector South headquarters with -- I'm sorry. My apologies, Mr. President. They did -- prior to that time, the ARSK did target the UN Sector South headquarters with mortar fire. So, after all is said and done, with the autopsies, investigations, and years of analysis by the Office of the Prosecutor, they were able to arguably establish one civilian, number 205, one civilian was possibly killed by artillery fire in Operation Storm. Despite this, despite this dearth and paucity of evidence, the Prosecution claims that the artillery incident is a criminal act, an unlawful attack against the civilian population for which General Gotovina is culpable. It is simply -- it's simply not borne out by any of the facts in the record. Frankly, the Prosecution employs this same tactic in many other instances, in which they engage in speculation over possible illicit inferences which could be drawn from their selection of evidence rather than meeting their burden of proof, which is to demonstrate that their conclusions are the only reasonable conclusions which could be drawn from the totality of the evidence. Yet they ask for the guilt of General Gotovina while offering this Chamber the evidence concerning the death of one individual, and even that, they don't lay out the factual circumstances of that death. Another example of how this tactic is employed by the Prosecution has to do with psy-ops. The Prosecution claims in paragraph 502 of their brief that P478 is an order by General Gotovina to drop flyers. However, the Prosecution's in-house expert, Mr. Theunens, makes clear that P478 was not - I emphasise - was not used during Operation Storm, notwithstanding what the Prosecution says in their brief. We refer the Chamber to Mr. Theunens's report, P113 -- excuse me, P1113, page 371, footnote 457. Mr. Theunens agreed that General Gotovina's actual order used during Storm, in D201, makes no mention of flyers. As outlined in our brief, and we shan't go into it at this juncture, at 320 -- paragraphs 320 to 329, the use of psy-ops was not the cause of the civilian evacuation or the fleeing of the area. These individuals left simply because of two reasons: They were encircled or going to be encircled, as told by General Mrksic; and as Mr. Strbac told us or verified in a tape, very strongly, that they left because they didn't want to stay under Croatian rule and they needed to "preserve their biological potential." And that's at D926. Notwithstanding the lack of evidence concerning flyers, Mr. Russo yesterday argued that, well, there is, in fact, proof that this flyer that we -- in evidence was in fact dropped. Really? Let us look at paragraphs 325 or 326 of the Gotovina Prosecution brief [sic]. The only evidence presented of a flyer being dropped was a flyer that was dropped in Bosnia. To try to counter this, Mr. Russo directs our attention to the testimony of Marija Vecerina, and he did that yesterday at page 33, line 1 to 5. What the Prosecution didn't tell you yesterday was that Ms. Vecerina never identified the flyer that was presented to her, and I point the Chamber to P62, paragraph 10; P653, paragraph 5. More importantly, Ms. Vecerina never testified that she and her family left the area because of the flyer. Instead, she testified that she left at the instruction of her son who told her he heard that -- he had heard over the radio that Knin had fallen. And that's why they left. And this can be found at trial transcript page 6727, line 24 to 25; and 6725, at line 19, through 6726, line 7. The Prosecution at no point has proven that Serb civilians left because of any unlawful use of either psy-ops or artillery. In the interests of time, Mr. President, I would like to move to the other factor alleged by the Prosecution in paragraph 21, which is the alleged acceptance by General Gotovina of crimes as justified acts of violence. The only thing I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, before you continue, could you clarify your reference to the paragraphs 325 and 326 of the -- to the Gotovina's Prosecution brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's the -- it's on a line -- it is our final brief, paragraphs 325 and 326 in our brief. I apologise.
