utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would like to turn our attention to this allegation of the -- our client's alleged acceptance of crime. Nothing could be further from the truth. In the few instances where this conversation came up, what did General Gotovina say? General Gotovina discussed this matter with the ECMM, as reflected in our brief, and the ECMM monitor who was present during this discussion understood several matters, that the police, civilian police, had control of the situation and that any person committing crimes should be charged. And next, he took away from that remark that General Gotovina wanted anyone, regardless of whether he was a soldier or a civilian, who was engaged in criminal behaviour to be charged with a crime. Remarkably, remarkably that is never discussed in the OTP's brief. However, as I refer back to Mr. Galovic, that is exactly what Mr. Galovic did when he came in and testified, over the course of the many months, where over 1200 charges were filed in the wake of Operation Storm. As I mentioned at the outset, an item that is conveniently, or whatever reason it happened to be, left out of the Prosecution's brief. We need not go into that significantly more than we have, and I refer the Chamber to paragraphs 593 to 599 of our brief to talk about General Gotovina's actions in the face of crime. But fundamentally, we challenge the statement of Mr. Hedaraly and the premise of the Prosecution where Mr. Hedaraly said yesterday most of these crimes were committed by soldiers or by civilians in concert with soldiers. Now, I understand that the -- that Your Honour has given us a chart that deals with the restrictions of movement in page 148 of the Prosecution's brief and we will discuss that. But prior to that, we need to discuss the fundamental flaw in the entire analysis by the Prosecution. And that is the attempt to designate all of these perpetrators or most of these perpetrators as members of the HV. And how do they do that? They do that by throwing the evidence of crimes that have taken place in the Krajina, in Sector South, and we did not debate at one point that crimes actually took place, and then putting it together with units that were located in the area at some time. And, a fortiori, because this took place, a crime took place and units may have been in the area at some time, a fortiori, they were responsible for that crime without ever identifying who the individual perpetrators were. And based on that, they're asking the Chamber to convict the accused. They are simply not anywhere near meeting their burden of proof. This underlying logical flaw was exemplified by all during the testimony of Prosecution witness William Hayden, when his conclusory statements and opinions elicited by the Prosecution were explored by the Defence counsel and the Chambers on cross. And I refer to Mr. Hayden's testimony at page 10628, line 15, through 10645, line 7. And without going into this in toto, Mr. President and Your Honours, I would like to summarise some of that. Mr. Hayden was drawing conclusions by systematic and organised looting and burning by the HV which upon examination were without foundation. Although he personally -- did not personally witness members of the HV involved in such activities, he concluded that the HV committed the crimes because he had not seen civilians in the area. This conclusion was reached by Mr. Hayden despite the fact that Mr. -- one Croatian official, Mr. Pasic, told Mr. Hayden that the crime was caused by civilians taking revenge. Mr. Hayden testified that while he considered the information provided by Mr. Pasic, he ruled it out -- he ruled out civilians as perpetrators of the crimes in the area. He did so despite having no information nor about -- nor investigation about how many civilians remained in the area after the Serb evacuation. How many civilians came back? This information was absolutely required before drawing his conclusion. As the Presiding Judge directed to Mr. Hayden at page 10634, lines 11 to 12, the Presiding Judge asked Mr. Hayden: "I'm not asking you what you saw." And referring to the lack of considering this information, Presiding Judge says: "I'm asking you whether you agree with me that this is a serious flaw in the reasoning." Mr. Hayden rejected that. Suffice it to say that the Prosecution has rejected this same matter. They've done the same exact thing. They have failed to ask, like Mr. Hayden, the following questions, simple questions, before contending that the only reasonable interpretation of the evidence was that HV members under the effective control of General Gotovina were the primary cause of these -- of crime. Did any of these crimes occur before Operation Storm? Were any civilians returned, had they returned to the area? When did they return and how many? Were the civilian police in the area, and military police? Did any of these categories of other people contribute to the problem? To the extent that people in uniform were observed, were they actual soldiers or did they have access to camouflage information? Were these people acting individually or with one another, or acting were they in an organised fashion, as a unit with a command and control structure? This is a fatal flaw in the presentation that is made by the Prosecution. If we turn to paragraph 479 of the Prosecution's brief, they argue that the vast majority of these crimes were carried out by HV soldiers, consistent with what Mr. Hedaraly said yesterday, that most of these crimes. Well, what does that mean? The vast majority of them were made. Most of these crimes were committed by the HV. The Prosecution conceded yesterday for the first time, at page 57, lines 13 through 15, that: "Civilians were involved in the commission of crimes." Okay. How many instances were they involved with and when and where? The Prosecution never tells us. Turning back to paragraph 479 of the Prosecution's brief where they note that a vast majority of these crimes were committed by the HV, they make several assumptions. They note that there was no mass return of Croat DPs until August 15th. Now let's look at the logic of that. There was no mass return, how many civilians or IDPs came back? How many civilians were in the area? Why would a mass return be required for crimes to be committed to civilians? How many returnees or criminals need to infiltrate the area before the Prosecution would consider the possibility that they have committed a crime? In pegging this return to August 15th, what they are trying to say is that there are no civilians coming in prior to the 15th, ergo, these are all HV soldiers and that General Gotovina must be responsible. I hasten to correct their errors in that regard. As shown by page 6 of Exhibit P352, page 2 -- excuse me, page 6 of P352, page 2 of D277, and page 1 of P805, and we detail this in our brief at paragraphs 482 and 498, civilians were coming back to this liberated area as early as the 6th of August. Internationals, on various different levels, report people coming back as of that date. This is essentially ignored by the Prosecution. Next, in that same allegation, they note that the -- that the military - and I'm talking about in their paragraph of 479 - that the military had full control of the area and check-points were established to prevent civilians from entering. We detail this in -- at paragraphs 464 to 469. But their own evidence contradicts that allegation. Look at the citations, as Mr. Tieger invited us to do, for that statement. It is Mr. Moric and Mr. Cipci, and both say that the restriction of movement in the area was done by civilians, the civilian police, not by the military police. Finally, the implicit reference in there that with check-points this area is going to be safe-guarded and sealed off is simply preposterous. As we see in paragraph 517 of the Gotovina brief, criminals like Bilic were getting around check-points easily because they knew the area. Mr. Galovic noted that it was impossible to have a check-point to close off this area. General Cross, who had experience with this in many different theatres said check-points in an area such as this would be impossible to foreclose people from getting in. In fact, there are even reports in this that we can detail where UNMOs, when faced with check-points, knew enough about the area to get around it. There is simply no basis in fact for this allegation that somehow check-points foreclosed people from coming into the area. Finally, of course, what the Prosecution tacitly agreed to was that after the 15th, there was a combination of civilians in there and that they were participating in this crime. But their answer to that is, and they cite the Chamber to paragraph 195 of the Martic appeal, was it really doesn't make a difference because they're part and parcel of -- they're working with the army and they're all guilty and Martic says so. Simply not true. A completely inaccurate cite which Your Honours directed us to. First of all, if we look at that, in that paragraph 195, the analysis was that the Trial Chamber found that these individuals that were committing these crimes were paramilitaries working in conjunction with the JNA and were -- could be directly tied to the accused, Mr. Martic, as part of his JCE liability. Such facts were never demonstrated here. The evidence that we have is that this criminal activity was disorganised, took place at various times and places, with people in uniforms operating in conjunction with civilians. The more appropriate analysis, I submit to Your Honours, is in paragraph -- or actually in paragraphs 191 to 193, and 197 to 200, where the Martic Appeals Chamber discussing this matters. And at paragraph 200, the Appeals Chamber notes as follows: "The Appeals Chamber concludes that the Trial Chamber erred in establishing a link between Martic and the perpetrators of these crimes. In particular, the Appeals Chamber finds that the origin of the armed men and their affiliation remains uncertain. Without any further elaboration on the affiliation of these armed men, no reasonable trier of fact could have held that the only reasonable conclusion in the circumstance was that these crimes could be imputed to a member of the JCE." Now, I add, Your Honours, that the Appeals Chamber drew this conclusion, despite the fact that the armed men were wearing camouflage and olive green uniforms at the time the crimes were made -- committed. We implore the Chamber to use this analysis when looking at the particular crimes that were levied by the Prosecution because they have not developed or made any connection by people in camouflage uniform that -- people committing crimes and have tied this back to General Gotovina as part of his chain of command and as his effective chain of command. Just briefly going through this restrictions of movement matter that was set forth on page 148 of the Prosecution's brief. Of course, the inference from this is that because there is a restriction of movement, that crimes were allowed to occur. This is -- this is mistaken on many different levels. First, of course, logically one would have to say that when restrictions of movement were in place, that crimes took place; and when restriction of movements didn't take place, crimes weren't taking place. Well, of course, there's no evidence on the record to support that at all. If we look at the various aspects of, for instance, Kistanje, is it the Prosecution's position based on P148 that HV members were only involved in criminal behaviour in Kistanje on the 11th of August and not before that and not after that? Absent the Prosecution taking that position, the juxtaposition of restriction of movement on the 11th of August with allegations of crime is irrelevant. The second flaw in the argument is that it was done to actually -- any restriction of movement was done to cover up crimes and we turn the Chamber to paragraphs 394 to 397 in our brief, where we talk about that, but what is instructive is one about Benkovac. There are two entries for Benkovac, on 7th of August and the 21st of August. If we look at what the entries are, any restriction of movement was not an attempt to cover up anything at all. What is cited for that restriction of movement is P112, and that's in footnote 12312. There, the UNMOs witness was not a cover-up or a tolerance for looting, but they report that MPs searching civilian vehicles driven by what appeared to be HV members and seizing items that appeared to be looted. This does not support a claim of criminal activity put in place because of a restriction of movement. Furthermore, as demonstrated by P1211, although problems did arise when HV members from the Benkovac area -- from the Benkovac area stayed in town drinking after its liberation, the commander of OG Zadar, by August 8th, issued an order forbidding HV members from entering Benkovac and town was put under control of the MP to prevent entry by HV and civilians. Lastly, when we look at many of these -- these restrictions of movement, restrictions of movement can be done for many different reasons. A restriction of movement that is done in Bosnia certainly was not done for anything other than restricting movement during a combat situation. Restrictions of movement were done by civilian police and even military police, people that are not under the chain of command of General Gotovina. What the Prosecution has failed to establish through this chart is that there was some correlation between a restriction of movement and crime. They simply throw out an issue of restriction of movement and maintain that some crime was taking place in the area and that there is some correlation between the both. I think what we have from the Martic Appeals Judgement is that that type of analysis does not suffice. Now I would like to turn to the murder count as laid out by Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, distinguished members of the Trial Chamber, I'm pleased and honoured to appear once again before you on behalf of General Gotovina. My colleagues have addressed the evidence in this case. I shall now set forth our concluding submissions on whether the Prosecution has proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt in light of the applicable law and elements of crimes. The defendant Ante Gotovina, a high-ranking military commander, is charged with widespread and systematic violations of humanitarian law. What is at the root of this law against which this Trial Chamber must measure his conduct. In 1952, shortly after the adoption of the Geneva Conventions in 1949, Sir Hersch Lauterpacht famously remarked that if international law is at a vanishing point of law, the law of war is perhaps even more conspicuously at the vanishing point of international law. In the shadow of the Second World War, Sir Hirsch Lauterpacht was referring to the basic challenge of imposing legal constraints on the waging of war. The basic challenge of humanising an inherently violent and inhumane activity. As Professor Kalshoven has explained, humanitarian law does not by any means purport to turn war into a fashionable and basically humane activity. Far more modestly, it aims to restrain the parties to an armed conflict from wanton cruelty and ruthlessness. Even so, war remains what it always was, a horrifying phenomenon. What lies at the root of the laws of war is a careful balance between humanitarian protection and military necessity. This balance was as relevant at the time of the 1863 Lieber Code as it is today. The former ICRC legal advisor, Louise Doswald-Beck, observed that the states negotiating Protocol I of 1977 had this balance firmly in mind so as to codify a law that was acceptable to their military staff. To codify a law that was acceptable to their military staff. Therein lies the viability of humanitarian law at the vanishing point of international law. It is a code of conduct acceptable to military commanders around the world because it does not ignore the horrifying realities of warfare. It may be tempting to expand humanitarian law's scope of protection by progressively diminishing the centuries' old balance with military necessity. It may be satisfying to develop the most exacting standards that can only be achieved by the best armies fighting in the best circumstances with the best weapons. A legal utopia that sanitises the horrifying realities of war. But a law that is unrealistic is also a law that is irrelevant. A law that is unrealistic would be ignored by the vast majority of military commanders around the word who are engaged in warfare, military commanders without the superior training and weaponry of the armed forces of the most advanced nations. In order to arrive at a conclusion of innocence or guilt, the Trial Chamber must determine whether General Gotovina acted reasonably, given the realities of the war that Croatia confronted. Those realities do not excuse crimes against civilians but humanitarian law does not require General Gotovina to do the impossible. It does not presuppose that he operated in ideal or hypothetical circumstances. It does not consider whether in hindsight reality was different than how it appeared to him at the time. It does not assume that faced with grave and imminent peril he had unlimited time and resources to train a professional army at the highest standards with the most sophisticated weaponry. All that humanitarian law demands of General Gotovina is that he acted reasonably, given the realities of the war that was waged on the newly independent Croatian nation. But that is not the standard underlying the Prosecution case. Throughout this proceeding, the Prosecution has stretched, distorted diluted or simply disregarded the law. It has done so to create a standard so exacting, so unrealistic, that it would result in General Gotovina's conviction no matter how reasonably he acted. It is a contrived standard that attempts to compensate for the insufficiency of the evidence that on any reasonable interpretation must result in an acquittal. Let us consider what the Prosecution's opening statement referred to as the core of its case. Namely, the allegation that a JCE existed to forcibly displace the Serbian civilian population through widespread and systematic unlawful shelling. At the pre-trial stage, the Defence Rule 72 submissions argued, consistent ICTY jurisprudence, that whether charged as war crimes or crimes against humanity, deportation and forceable transfer only apply to territories under the actual control of an opposing belligerent. We submitted that the allegations of unlawful shelling, prior to the liberation of so-called Krajina, could only be charged as unlawful attacks and not deportation. In response, the Prosecution argued vigorously that such a charge was not required because the definition of deportation under the laws of war is inapplicable to crimes against humanity. The Prosecution then abruptly changed its position and amended Count 1 of the indictment to add what we still maintain is a new charge of persecutory unlawful attacks against civilians and civilian objects. The Prosecution now admits that to constitute an actus reus of crimes against humanity, shelling can only be unlawful if it violates the laws of war. But the Prosecution final brief completely ignores the authorities at paragraph 860 of the Defence final brief on the exclusion of preoccupation hostilities from the law of deportation. At paragraph 482 of its brief, the Prosecution persists in the theory that unlawful shelling prior to occupation satisfies the requirements of deportation. Now, consistent with paragraph 11 of its pre-trial brief, the Prosecution's final brief confirms at paragraph 486 that only "few civilians" did not flee the shelling attack. Thus, the Prosecution Brioni JCE theory rests entirely on proof beyond a reasonable doubt of mass expulsion resulting from widespread or systematic unlawful shelling prior to Croatia's liberation of the Krajina territory. Furthermore, it rests on a finding by this Trial Chamber that the law on deportation includes preoccupation hostilities contrary to ICTY jurisprudence and humanitarian law. On both counts we submit the Prosecution's core JCE theory manifestly fails. Let us disregard for a moment the profound legal flaws in the Prosecution theory and assume that preoccupation shelling can be a modality of deportation. The evidence of unlawful shelling is still so grossly inadequate that one has to ask how the Prosecution could pursue such a charge in this case. The Prosecution's submissions yesterday conjured images of Stalingrad in the Second World War, of cities and towns reduced to rubble, and innocent civilians massacred by indiscriminate shelling. So this Trial Chamber has to ask, after 15 years of investigation and in view of such bold allegations, where is the evidence of this massive atrocity? Why is there no proof whatsoever that even a single civilian died as a result of unlawful shelling? Where are the photographs of Knin reduced to rubble? Why are the positive findings of the UNMO and UN CIVPOL investigations simply ignored? The Prosecution case is simply hopeless. There is no case to answer. But instead of doing what is right and dropping these baseless charges, the Prosecution has persisted in diluting humanitarian law in attempting to blur the boundary between war crimes and the unfortunate realities of war. At paragraph 484 of its brief, the Prosecution states that civilians who were the object of the attack, as well as observers from international organisation, uniformly described the terrifying effect of the attack. In oral argument yesterday, Mr. Russo repeatedly spoke of the hours of panic and uncertainty that civilians suffered while cowering in their basement. But to point out that war creates fear, panic and uncertainty is to state the obvious. It is not a substitute for proof of unlawful attacks. It is self-evident that neither civilians, nor combatants, for that matter, particularly enjoy artillery attacks. All that this line of reasoning demonstrates is a profound misunderstanding of the exacting proof required for conduct of hostilities violations under humanitarian law. In arriving at its legal findings on the core allegations in this case, the Trial Chamber must consider its far-reaching consequences on armed forces around the world. Should NATO military commanders in Afghanistan stop using artillery when Taliban insurgents hide in civilian areas? Should they fear war crimes convictions as the Prosecution seeks in this case? What about armed forces without weapons capable of the same degree of precision as NATO forces? We submit, respectfully, that if on these facts General Gotovina can be found guilty of unlawful shelling and mass deportation, then any military commander anywhere could be held guilty. A conviction on these facts would make lawful warfare impossible. In effect, it would defeat the very purpose of humanitarian law by equating the inherent horrors of war with war crimes. There is yet another fundamental flaw in the Brioni JCE theory. The Prosecution brief admits at paragraph 482 that unless there is proof of widespread unlawful shelling, the deportation counts fail insofar as there must be proof of forcible displacement without grounds permitted in international law. But the more fundamental problem is that there is no proof even that Serb civilians fled in panic because of lawful artillery attacks. Even if we assume that this lawful attack had terrifying effects, a reasonable inference from the evidence is that the civilian population left because of the RSK's own anti-Croat propaganda and evacuation orders. Even the Prosecution witness Ambassador Galbraith testified that the side effect of the war was the departure but not the expulsion of the Serbs. To the best of my knowledge, this is the first prosecution ever in the history of international law where mass evacuation is equated with mass expulsion. Absent widespread unlawful attacks, to argue that Operation Storm was the cause of the exodus would be tantamount to saying that Croatia had no right to win the war because it would result in RSK evacuation orders. That would have to be the logic. In this regard, it is remarkable that a significant element of the Prosecution's JCE theory is denial of the immediate mass return of the evacuated Serbs. At paragraph 35 of its brief, the Prosecution states that, and I quote: "Led by Tudjman, the Croatian leadership adopted a no-mass-return policy, refusing to process group applications for return." Let us examine this argument in light of humanitarian law. As set forth in paragraphs 569 to 571 of the Defence brief, it is well established in international law that states have the right to expel enemy aliens during armed conflict. In response to the Trial Chamber's question, Mr. Tieger explained yesterday that the authorities we've cited are inapplicable to the facts of this case. In particular, he argued that the Eritrea-Ethiopia Claims Commission Award held that mass expulsion of enemy aliens without individualised determinations are unlawful. I had the privilege of arguing that case before a tribunal presided by Professor van Houtte, and I can assure the Tribunal that this is a correct understanding of the award. But we are not invoking this authority to justify a non-existent mass expulsion. We are only pointing out that if it is within Croatia's sovereign rights to expel enemy aliens, then it follows logically that Croatia is not under an obligation to allow their immediate mass return during an armed conflict. This is clearly a legitimate measure of national security, and it is difficult to imagine any state in similar circumstances anywhere in the world that would allow a policy of mass return for enemy aliens. The Prosecution has not denied that the FRY was engaged in armed conflict with Croatia, which it considered to be an illegitimate state. It is not denied that FRY RSK citizens were not and did not consider themselves to be citizens of Croatia. It may be argued that in relation to Croatia's succession to the SFRY it had a customary law obligation to allow habitual residents that would otherwise become stateless the right to apply for Croatian citizenship. But obviously those that pledged allegiance to the FRY RSK and rejected Croatian sovereignty became enemy aliens. That was exactly the finding the Eritrea-Ethiopia Claims Commission in relation to dual Eritrea-Ethiopian nationals habitually resident in Ethiopia. The present case is even more forceful because, unlike the case of Ethiopia, the FRY RSK citizens were not dual nationals of Croatia. There was no question whatsoever about their allegiance to a hostile state that occupied a third of Croatia. Under such circumstances, it is total obvious that Croatia was under no obligation to allow their immediate mass return. It is astonishing that this fundamental rule of humanitarian law was never considered by the Prosecution until its closing argument in this case. It is yet another demonstration of the profound flaws in its JCE theory. That is to say, transforming a perfectly lawful no-mass-return policy into evidence of criminal intention. Another observation relates to the characterisation of armed conflict issue. Mr. Tieger yesterday confirmed the Prosecution's view that there is "extensive evidence" that the armed conflict is international rather than internal. We fully concur with this view and paragraphs 44 to 49 of our brief sets forth the facts that satisfy the overall control test of the Tadic Appeals Judgement. The problem is that the Prosecution has never pleaded an international armed conflict in the indictment. Paragraph 56 of the indictment only states that at all relevant times a state of armed conflict existed in the Krajina region of the Republic of Croatia. The Prosecution can therefore only rely on a non-international armed conflict to satisfy the nexus required for all counts in the indictment. The authority for this proposition is the Hadzihasanovic Appeals Chamber decision, pursuant to Rule 72(E), as to validity of appeal, dated 21 February 2003. The decision states in relevant part at paragraphs 11 to 12 that, and I quote: "If the Prosecution wishes to rely upon an international armed conflict, it must plead as a material fact that the armed conflict was international in character and state the basis upon which such an assertion is made. The Prosecution should not be permitted to rely upon the imprecision of its current pleading in order to put forward a case that the armed conflict was international in character without a further amendment to its indictment to make this expressly clear." And I note that decision related only to Article 3 charges. There were no Article 2 charges involved. In this case, the Prosecution has expressly stipulated that the conflict is international, but that is in direct contradiction with its pleading in the indictment that the conflict is non-international. As Hadzihasanovic indicates, it must satisfy the nexus requirement of all charges based on its pleading that the conflict is non-international. It is difficult to see, Mr. President, how the Prosecution can reconcile this contradiction to sustain its charges. With a fundamental core of the Brioni JCE theory in Counts 1 to 3 eliminated, a final consideration is whether the Prosecution can still salvage its case with respect to remaining acts of plunder, wanton destruction, murder, and cruel and inhumane acts in Count 4 to 9 of the indictment. We submit that it cannot. Since there is no proof of a JCE to commit mass expulsion, it is difficult to see how there could be a reasonable inference that there was a JCE to commit other post-Storm crimes, such as burning and looting, that the Prosecution claims were foreseeable within the scope of JCE category 3, as we heard yesterday. If there is no Brioni JCE category 1 or 2, with respect to mass expulsion, as claimed by the Prosecution, then a derivative JCE category 3 is simply irrelevant. Furthermore, the Prosecution does not plead any JCE other than that at Brioni. A further consideration that neither a persecutory policy nor the widespread or systematic element of Article 5 charges can be inferred from a mere crime wave. The Prosecution refers throughout its brief to a post-Storm crime wave. As set forth in paragraph 819 of the Defence brief, states negotiating the ICC Rome Statute did not consider a mere crime wave to qualify as crimes against humanity and customary law. Consistent with the Kupreskic Trial Judgement, the ICC elements of crime stipulates that although a formal policy is not required, there must be at least "a deliberate failure to take action which is consciously aimed at encouraging such attack." This is an onerous threshold that cannot be easily satisfied. It is not sufficient to demonstrate that Croatia did not plan adequately for the liberation of occupied territories or that it had limited resources, or even that it had limited enthusiasm to prevent and punish crimes in the face of other wartime priorities. The only reasonable inference must be that there was a deliberate failure to act consciously aimed at encouraging such crimes, and we submit that the Prosecution has failed to prove that case beyond a reasonable doubt. Mr. President, I just want to advise the Chamber that the Cermak Defence team has kindly agreed to give me an additional five minutes, so I will be wrapping up with that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which means that you have, then, five minutes left. Or would that be seven. Let's not talk in terms of seconds. It may be clear to the parties that we want to conclude the first round of Defence submissions and their final argument today. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: As set forth by my colleagues, the evidence demonstrates that the UN Special Representative Akashi and other credible authorities did not consider the burning and lootings to be part of a systematic campaign. The evidence demonstrates further that Croatia did not tolerate this crime wave which resulted from lawless in the wake of the RSK'S sudden collapse. Officials were clearly embarrassed by this conduct which tarnished Croatia's international reputation. Notwithstanding the chaos of war, there were repeated orders and other measures including 1300 prosecutions to prevent and punish such crimes. In this light, the allegation that there was a deliberate policy of failing to act consciously aimed at encouraging such crimes is certainly not the only reasonable inference that can be drawn. To accept the Prosecution argument that a JCE is the only reasonable inference, the Trial Chamber would have to conclude that this was the conspiracy of the century, an act of such diabolic genius that a criminal policy permeating the entire Croatian state left no trace whatsoever. Of course, irrespective of whether there was a joint criminal enterprise or not, the only possible basis for General Gotovina's contribution to post-Storm crimes, whether under article 7(1) or 7(3), would be what Mr. Gustafson alleged to be his deliberate persistent inaction. But once again, the Prosecution interprets humanitarian law so unrealistically that nothing that General Gotovina did could possibly be sufficient. The Prosecution's basic allegation is that the many measures he took were merely a cover-up. As Ms. Gustafson argued, Gotovina expected his orders to fail. The absurdity of this case is demonstrated by paragraph 125 of the Prosecution's brief, where it is argued that in issuing his attack order, and I quote: "Gotovina knew that his superficial instructions to prevent looting and burning and generic references to the Geneva Conventions were manifestly inadequate measure to prevent these crimes in the circumstances." Presumably, the Prosecution view is that humanitarian law requires military commanders to issue exhaustive scholarly dissertations on the Geneva Conventions. Only then could orders to protect civilians qualify as necessary and reasonable measures. The argument is plainly ridiculous. The Prosecution would further maintain that General Gotovina's scathing condemnation of drinking and looting among soldiers that he referred to as barbarians was all a cover-up. Presumably his anger at his subordinates was meant to encourage undisciplined conduct among his troops on the eve of his next war with Ratko Mladic in Bosnia. To argue that this is only reasonable inference can that be drawn is simply ridiculous. It is also astonishing that Ms. Gustafson would state that there is no difference between the duties of operational commanders and other commander in disregard of the authorities in paragraphs 647 to 649 of our brief. In the landmark High Command Trial, the US Military Tribunal recognised even with respect to monstrous Nazi crimes, that an operational commander such as General Wilhelm von Leeb had the right to leave administrative duties in occupied territories to his rear -- to his subordinate commanders and to assume that they would see to their proper execution. Given the radically different context of Nazi crimes and Operation Storm, General Gotovina should surely deserve no less than General von Leeb. In this regard and in closing, I must express my appreciation for Ms. Gustafson's analogy to what parents or authority figures should do when their orders are disregarded. As a father of two naughty children, Mr. President, I have issued repeated orders against mischief. But now that I'm in The Hague pleading before this Chamber, I rest assured that the implementation of those orders is the responsibility of others back in Montreal. And our expectation should be no different with respect to General Gotovina who had to assume that as operational commander of 30.000 soldiers, responsible for two theatres of war in Croatia and Bosnia, having done his utmost to instill discipline and professionalism in his soldiers in exceedingly difficult wartime circumstances, that he could issue orders and assume that others would see to the proper execution. The Prosecution has repeatedly asked this Trial Chamber to look at the totality of the evidence in arriving at its conclusion. We welcome this invitation because when the overall circumstances of the war are considered, General Gotovina's efforts to establish a disciplined and professional army while confronted with a ruthless enemy that had ethnically cleansed and occupied a third of Croatia, an enemy that regularly bombed its cities and towns with impunity, to consider that in the face of such a grave and imminent peril, in the shadow of Srebrenica and the threatened fall of Bihac to yet another genocide, if the totality of these circumstances are considered, the argument that he failed to take necessary and reasonable measures cannot possibly be the only reasonable inference under any realistic view of humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, you have to -- I said I would be strict. Apparently you --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I have been handed a note, sir, that the Markac team has also given me an additional five minutes, and I have literally less than that to conclude my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What you're actually doing, you just, although at a higher speed, continue to read what you had prepared. If you have limited time, you have to adapt your situation and perhaps take out some of the rhetorics, whether -- for example, whether it is the conspiracy of the decade or century is not really very convincing for the Chamber. But it's up to you to use your time, but if you just continue to do what you are doing, more or less ignoring, you have three minutes left. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: General Gotovina has spent almost five years of his life in prison on charges that are wholly without merit. He is a courageous and honourable soldier to whom we owe a debt of gratitude. Gratitude for risking his life to defeat those that inflicted the scourge of ethnic cleansing on the peoples of the former Yugoslavia. Gratitude for making it possible for this Tribunal to arrest those most responsible for such unspeakable atrocities. Amidst the horrifying realities of the war that he fought and by any reasonable measure of humanitarian law, justice demands that he be declared innocent of the baseless accusations against him. In conclusion, Mr. President, honourable members of the Chamber, we respectively submit that this Trial Chamber should enter a judgement of acquittal for General Gotovina on all counts of the indictment. I thank you for your patience and attention. That concludes my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akhavan. Who is next in line? It will be the Cermak Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I don't have to remind you that you shouldn't speak too quickly but I still would expect you and the Markac Defence to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We just have some furniture arrangements to deal with, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay, it is my intention to have a break starting in 20 minutes from now. A break of, then, 20 minutes again until quarter to 1.00. If you would find a more appropriate moment, please feel free within certain limits to choose that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour. Your Honour, this is the closing argument on behalf of Ivan Cermak. At a stage in the case, it having started in March 2008 with the opening of the Prosecution, calling of witnesses, and then a considerable period of time later, the closing arguments to be presented, and we're able to look back through the corridor of that time and take an assessment of what was said the day Mr. Tieger opened the case, what had been written in an indictment before the opening of the case, what had been written in a pre-trial brief by the Prosecution, the allegations that they were to make, and we look back now to see whether they have been proved or not, what has changed, whether there's been any substance to support those allegations. At the start of the trial, they were relying upon statements taken in the English language, Croatian witnesses not having statements in their own language, witnesses who had made statements subsequently came into court and were accountable in a trial for what they had said, and an examination of what they had said to investigators took place. And during that period of time, there was some telling moments. I'm just going to identify four, because they concern the Cermak case, and they were telling moments that show that the case that was to be presented was not the case that came about in fact. And they showed a Prosecution that was on the run with its allegations. It had started with broad allegations of General Cermak being in command of umpteen divisions of the Split Military District. It had started with allegations of him being in command and control of everything that moved in and around Knin and Sector South. Is that where they have come to, that same position when Mr. Carrier addressed you yesterday? Did he have that convincing confidence about a man who'd proved his case? Looking at the final brief, when you read it, analyse the allegations that have been made, look at the footnotes, not ours, but look at the Prosecution footnotes and see what is cited in support. Are those citations correct, reflect what has been written in the main document, or false? And I'll use that word, because that's a word that came up in the Prosecution final brief about evidence from the Cermak Defence. It's not a word I would generally use in court but it was one we took exception to in the final brief from the Prosecutor. And we heard it again yesterday. Let no one doubt we will meet fire with fire. But those telling moments, let's just have a look at those. When General Lausic was to give evidence before this Court, the night before he met the Prosecution investigator. He was furtively handed a brown envelope. I don't know whether it was furtive or not but it sounded like it from his description. And in that envelope were documents, and one of those documents was the Exhibit D34, the organisational order of 1993, concerning garrisons. This was a document that had not been mentioned by Mr. Lausic in his considerable interviews as a suspect with the Prosecutor, not been mentioned in his statement that had been prepared from those interviews by the Prosecutor, and suddenly, someone in the Prosecution team must have thought, We've dropped a clanger here. We have made a big error in our assessment of what is relevant in the evidence in this case. Because Lausic's failure to address the key document concerning the authority and powers of the garrison commander was missing, it wasn't referred to, and it was significant that the Prosecution expert, Theunens, had only mentioned that document in one page of his voluminous expert report. That was a telling moment of a Prosecutor on the run, trying somehow to get an advantage from an important witness in relation to an important exhibit. Another telling moment, the second I will refer to, in relation to another key witness. For this, the Gotovina team will take credit and that's why I gave them the extra five minutes. They wanted Mr. Theunens's draft of his reports. It was not something that we were interested in. We were content to contest Mr. Theunens on the report we had before us. But that was instructive, because that draft report, two weeks before it was finalised, showed such substantial and substantive changes concerning the case involving Mr. Cermak that his whole position in this trial had to be re-written by the Prosecution expert to support the constructed indictment against Mr. Cermak. We spent a few days finding out about the drafts. We spent a few days analysing the drafts, but the product of it, we are grateful for, because, in our view, it was a telling moment. The next telling moment was when Mr. Dzolic came to give evidence. He'd been the commander of the Knin Company of the military police for one week in Knin. When you look at his statement, it's very curiously written, as we've set out in our final brief, to establish some kind of authority or that he was expected to obey orders from General Cermak to try and make some kind of command connection. You look at the paragraph concerned, number 34, and you can see it's entirely unconvincing as the sort of document this Court has to rely upon. But when he came to give evidence and had to be accountable for what he had said, he resiled from what he had said to the Prosecution, and he presented an entirely different picture of the evidence. A telling moment. The same telling moment came about with the witness P-086. Exactly the same issues, and exactly the same matter arose. Outside the comfort of the statements that had been taken years before and when made accountable in court, those witnesses did not provide evidence upon which the Prosecution had tried to establish the foundation of their case against Mr. Cermak. In this review that I'm doing in general terms of the case, I refer the Court to the Defence evidence called by -- on behalf of Mr. Cermak in this trial. When you look at the Prosecution final brief, it is staggering that major parts of evidence are simply not dealt with by argument. When witnesses were called by the Cermak Defence, similarly, it was staggering that there was no challenge to the substance of the evidence. And the reason why that happened was because the evidence that we called was actually the truth of the matter. You were receiving evidence from experts who knew what they were talking about, from people who had been associated with the appointment of Mr. Cermak, from people who were in Knin and present and saw him work, and from those who had also explained this years before to the Prosecution, the good intentions of Mr. Cermak and the nature of his work. When one reviews the cross-examination of those witnesses and the matters of substance, the challenges to them are very, very limited. And the reason for that is this. The reason is that they were telling the truth. Take the expert witness General Feldi. He was a man who intimately knew the service regulations that are an important document in this trial; Exhibit P32. He was a man who knew about garrisons in the Croatian Army. His expertise and why he was called as a witness were apparent. More time was spent, it seemed - may not have been the case but it seemed - dealing with matters of his credibility rather than the substance of what he had to say. Defence expert witness, Pero Kovacevic, a man who had written the regulations, responsible for drafting the laws of the Croatian Army, knew what he was talking about, which is why he was brought here as an expert witness. Time again spent on his credibility but the substance of his expert's report not challenged. General Deverell, the same. Mr. Albiston, the same. And what we ask the Court to do, echoing the words of Mr. Tieger, is that although we have called substantial Defence evidence, it is entitled to the same status as any other evidence in this case, and we ask that this Court consider the totality of the evidence, because it is through that totality that the Court, in fact, will arrive at a truthful and just verdict. A few words now generally about General Cermak's position. How did he arrive in Knin. We know from the evidence that his presence was not planned. I'll be addressing the Court about the latest Brioni theory that the Prosecution advanced at a late stage of the final brief in this case. He arrived almost as an accident, a consequent of events, that he was given the call and asked to attend the president and given his task to go to Knin. A task for which he had not been prepared, trained, nor given power and authority of any sufficient degree or at all. The Prosecution claim that, whilst in Knin, General Cermak, as with other members of the JCE, had permitted a climate of impunity, that he had allowed crimes to happen. And this begs the question then of what did he do. You have heard substantial evidence in this case that he not only condemned crimes publicly, he condemned crimes privately. He condemned crimes at meetings in the garrison. Is that the activity of someone who is a member of a JCE? What would be the point of him permitting a climate of impunity if he was against the fact that crimes were happening and he was expressing that to others? In sum, it doesn't add up. And what has happened here is that three generals have been wanted to go on trial, and his name has come up. He is a person who was in the wrong place at the wrong time and had done no wrong. Why was General Cermak sent there? His experience in business, logistics, spoken of by many who gave evidence here, his ability to organise, and obviously in the confused situation in the liberated town of Knin at that time, a man of his qualities was needed to try and normalise life. And that, Your Honours, was exactly what General Cermak sought to do. I'm now going to go directly to various allegations that the Prosecution have made concerning General Cermak and his appointment. It was alleged by Mr. Carrier and in the final brief that his role was envisaged at the Brioni meeting; Exhibit P461, page 27. If you go to that document to look at that allegation, firstly, the context of the conversation concerns the imminent conflict and war. It is nothing to do with the situation after the conflict has ended. There is no mention within the context of that conversation that General Cermak was going to have a position in Knin, and certainly not that he would be handling complaints and neutralising interventions from UNCRO. The exact text is this. We need a staff for relations with UNCRO, a permanent liaison who would resolve things with them, for us to get instructions because matters will evolve too rapidly. The president stated that this person would have to be linked to his office. And at page 29, he linked that -- he named that person, Mr. Sarinic. This is a question to be dealt with, what you just said and also in reference to UNCRO, and this means Sarinic. What I'd like to know is whether it is safer to coordinate and manage affairs from Brioni or Zagreb. Absolutely nothing to do with this manufactured context put by the Prosecution in their final brief concerning Mr. Cermak in Knin. But it's interesting why they felt they needed to construct some kind of link pre-liberation of Knin. And the reason is this. They simply didn't have any evidence of him being part of a JCE. They have attempted to create a notion in the case, to bolster a weak case, to try and make it stronger. Moving from that issue concerning the allegation that General Cermak had been considered or someone in his position to take over a role handling complaints and neutralising interventions from UNCRO to the next part of the attempt to make the appointment of General Cermak to Knin as the garrison commander appear in some way sinister, and this concerns the presidential appointment. The allegation is made that the ordinary rules of the appointments procedure were circumvented to enable Mr. Cermak to take up his position. Well, the procedure for appointments was explained by the military expert, General Feldi at D1673, pages 43 to 44. And his appointment complies with the constitution of Croatia and the laws on defence which requires that the president shall appoint and dismiss generals. Our submission, the fact that the president appointed General Cermak, in fact, indicates that his role was to be a different role, not the role envisaged by the Prosecution, but the role of normalising life in Knin and the role of helping the international organisation in Knin. Nothing more, nothing less, nothing further, and certainly not part of a planned criminal enterprise. The idea was to appoint General Cermak to a job that was essentially outside the Croatian armed forces, not within the usual structure of the Split Military District, nor the Croatian armed forces command, and to be a job of a short duration and a job which was necessary and needed after liberation. Nowhere in any of the discussions, in any of the documents, in any of the statements, is there a single reference to General Cermak's work being solely for the return of Croats to the region. He never said it, no one else said it. His job was of an entirely general nature and normalisation meant normalisation for everybody, nothing more or nothing less, and never was his position conceived as being a way of causing others to leave the area or cause others to commit crimes against Serbs. To try and add to the sinister nature of the appointment, and to try and give some sort of argument that they can put forward to this Court, Prosecution final brief, paragraph 289, the context of Cermak's appointment is put this way. On the 4th of August, 1995, Susak briefed Tudjman on Storm's progress, prompting - and that's the added word - prompting Tudjman to request that Cermak be contacted. Well, the man who was there, Mr. Radin, never said that, and neither was it ever put to him that somehow Minister Susak was connected with Mr. Cermak's appointment. It simply has been put into this case to try and add a bit of prejudice and to make you think that there is a sinister reason behind the appointment of General Cermak to Knin. His appointment as the garrison commander had nothing to do with Minister Susak. Nothing to do with any sinister tasks. Again, a picture is sought to be constructed that Cermak was somehow a trusted insider. And that's the phrase that -- that's used. It's not one that was put to Mr. Radin, Mr. Vidosevic, Mr. Skegro, any other witnesses, that he was a trusted insider. And that is being fed to you this way, because they want to make you think that he is part of a JCE. And that phrase "trusted insider" is something that arises from a newspaper article involving the former General Cervenko who described Cermak as the president's personal man of confidence. However, that General Cervenko rejected that interview that he gave the very next day, at D1306. And that's an important fact that you would have thought the Prosecution would have sought to deal with in some substantive way. But when you look at it, and as it was put to General Deverell, this is gossip. This isn't substantive information. This is something of no real consequence. So, the Prosecution are attempting to also build a picture of General Cermak as a trusted insider, having close personal ties to President Tudjman and other members of the JCE. Your Honour, I will go on to that topic now, as it is the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. We will have a break, and we will resume at five minutes to 1.00, sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Moving on to a trusted insider who had close personal ties, where is the evidence of any meetings that Mr. Carrier referred to yesterday? It's not good enough to come into this courtroom and say there were public and private meetings. What -- of what? Where? The meetings that we have seen evidence of in the Presidential transcripts do not reflect adversely upon Mr. Cermak in any way. That is the evidence and they show the nature of his tasks and work. They don't show anything more or anything less. So coming into this courtroom to mention public and private meetings at which things would have been discussed is simply not good enough to build a criminal case, and the fact of the matter is they simply didn't happen. We have the evidence of the meetings and what was said, and that is where it is. In relation to other alleged members of the JCE, where is the foundation for the close personal ties between the other alleged members and General Cermak? That has not been the subject of evidence of any significant nature. What we do know is that General Cermak said in his interview he knew Mr. Jarnjak personally. He referred to him as a friend. He referred to General Markac as a friend. He said his relations with President Tudjman were good in 1993; but when he left government, at that stage, afterwards, there was little contact between 1993 and 1995. They saw each other two or three times. In relation to the other alleged members of the JCE, General Cervenko, Ademi, others, Mr. Radin, where is it? Where is this foundation that somehow General Cermak came into an inner circle whereby he was given sufficient trust that he would go on to help and support the commission of crimes? It's simply not there. If it had been there, we would have been able to have dealt with it. In fact, the evidence shows that there was very good reason why General Cermak was chosen to go to Knin, and the citations in the footnotes of the Prosecution brief actually support those good reasons that were cited by Mr. Vedris, that he was to encourage the organisation of civilian life in the area and town of Knin. Tudjman tried to find a person who had organisational skills, who could initiate rebuilding the area. Mr. Radin simply did not say that the -- that the president did not mention anybody else as a possible alternative. There's no evidence as to what was in the president's thought. The opportunity to put him on trial about these matters passed a long while ago. We simply don't know. Mr. Skegro and Mr. Vidosevic, likewise, emphasised the skills of Mr. Cermak which were appropriate to be employed down in Knin from that time to try and restore an area that was to be the subject of an influx of people who'd been excluded from it for over four years, as well as to encourage the people who were there to stay and those who had self-evacuated to come back. And I will be dealing with that in a little bit more detail later on. In the conversation that General Cermak had with the president in 1999, at Exhibit P1144, that conversation clearly indicates the extent of General Cermak's work and never once did it include responsibility for law and order. It did not include responsibility for the police, the military, or anything else. That was never put to him by the president. It is an informal conversation where neither would have suspected, one would think, that such a tape would end up in a court of law ten years later. But nowhere within that statement was there any suggestion that General Cermak had, in some way, not fulfilled his task in normalisation, his task in reconstruction; but nowhere is it stated that he was responsible for the law enforcement in the area and responsible to have prevented crimes that happened. It's interesting that the Prosecution state that Cermak's appointment and role was almost also immediately circulated among Croatian officials, including senior members of the political leadership, the military, and the police. There's simply no source cited that can support that, and, indeed, what the evidence reveals is that Cermak was introduced into the power structures of either the police or the power structures of the military. He was sent there on his sole and lone mission to carry out the tasks that he been given. Nothing more, nothing less. The appointment had been discussed at the meeting when VONS members were present, no introduction into the power structures. And in fact, as Mr. Vedris told the Court, transcript page 23670, he heard the announcement on the radio and he called Mr. Cermak, and this is interesting because it shows the state of mind of Mr. Cermak at that time. In an informal conversation, Mr. Cermak told him he'd accepted the appointment and he'd accepted to help. This was role of helping, not a role of anything else, or that a matter that would further advance this prosecution. The senior police officer in the area, Mr. Cipci, who saw General Cermak arrive in Knin on the 6th, asked Mr. Jarnjak what Mr. Cermak's function was. Again, that hardly constitutes the issue of some presidential directive, in some form or other, circulated amongst senior Croatian officials as to Mr. Cermak's responsibility and role. I have touched on the importance of Mr. Cermak's role in the normalisation of life. What we have now in this case, because that has been absolutely and thoroughly proved and established by the Defence in the course of this trial, is that the Prosecution have attempted to change the nature of that task from normalisation, simple, the only phrase that was ever used, to add on, in their submissions, that it was to facilitate "the return of Croats" to the area through infrastructure protection, sanitation, mine clearance, et cetera. Now, the issuing of colonisation as being Mr. Cermak's task and job was, again, never put to people like Mr. Radin, Mr. Skegro, Mr. Pasic, all the people who were there at the time. It was simply not a concept because that would have been met with a straight rejection by anyone, if it had been put by the Prosecution, because the weight of this evidence is overwhelmingly in favour of the fact that it was normalisation, full stop. He was nothing to do with Operation Return. He was nothing to do with the MUP structure which was administering Operation Return. This concept that has been brought into this case is, again, a last-ditch attempt to try and make valid evidence invalid and criminally liable, and in our submission to the Court, it simply doesn't work. If one goes to the statements of two witnesses who had their evidence in private session, protected witnesses, if we could go into private session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to go through all the detail of normalisation which is adequately set out in the Defence final brief, but I'm going to turn to another subject that was introduced in relation to General Cermak to say that his contact with the international community was in order to appease or contain international observers; paragraph 289 of the Prosecution final brief, and as stated by Mr. Carrier. Well, if we consider the point of contact and what happened when Mr. Cermak dealt with the international organisations, we need to make it clear that he was not the only person to whom international organisations went. Knin police book, D57, logs reports crimes from UNCRO. Witness P-086 testified UNCIVPOL informing of crimes. Numerous international organisation reports of crimes record that they will contact the local policija. P11, P226, P232, P234, P235, P238, P247, P251, P260, P262. But there were also reports of what happened from the international organisations to both Mr. Cermak, as well as the local police. There was not by any means any sort of exclusive relationship that was constructed in order to prevent information going down the line to the correct authorities with the responsibility to deal with crime. UNCIVPOL even set up a cooperation system with the local police, as we see at D53. The Prosecution allege Mr. Cermak contained reports of crime. Well, that is simply incorrect. Certainly in the case they presented that was the attempt to construct an allegation against him, but as we know from the statements of Mr. Rincic, Exhibit D1680, para 20; Mr. Lukavic, D1687, paragraph 54; D1688, paragraph 37. Mr. Dondo, D1695, paragraph 17, paragraph 19; D1696, paragraph 7 and 24. Pasic, D1706, paragraphs 4 to 5. There was clear evidence that Mr. Cermak not only condemned crimes and didn't approve of it and wanted it stopped when he was present and spoke in briefings, but also that he passed on information that he had received from the international organisations to the military police and local police. So, these key allegations of appeasement containing filtering reports to prevent and soak up just within himself what he was being told by international observers is simply not made out on the evidence. Not only that. We have seen letters from Mr. Cermak passing on information of a report of crimes from the International Red Cross, from Mr. Forand, from whomsoever, sending them as letters to Mr. Romanic, to Mr. Cetina. D1756 is even marked Cetina, urgent. That's not the conduct of a man preventing the flow of information, doing nothing about it. That is the conduct of a man fulfilling the proper tasks of a citizen, as he was supposed to do and which he complied with. Now, the allegation that he was preventing information from getting to the Croatian forces or the Croatian authorities, be they the Ministry of Interior or elsewhere, simply doesn't hang together when one considers the voluminous number of orders to stop crime set out in the Cermak Defence Annex A of the final brief, where information was certainly going to the highest authorities that there was trouble in the area. Constructing this case in a way to make it totally centred around Mr. Cermak in Knin is a disservice to the evidence. Those orders that were issued by higher authorities and at all levels were part of a concerted attempt by the authorities to try and deal with a problem that had developed after the liberation of the area, and it is simply wrong to try and make it a picture that General Cermak was preventing information from passing freely. It was simply not the case. We know from evidence in the case that the Croatian Army liaison officers who had pre-existing channels with UNCRO and international organisations were also receiving information directly. That information was being passed to their commander, Brigadier Plestina, in Zagreb, who even went to visit Knin and also discussed with UNCRO directly in Zagreb issues that had arisen from the international organisations. General Cermak's willingness to help, and that's what he said to Mr. Vedris when he told him he was going down to Knin, I'm going to help, and his willingness to go and see the international community, has an utterly reasonable explanation that we submit cannot be rejected in favour of the Prosecution theory, that he was taking it on himself to contain this information and not pass it on. It is utterly reasonable to a man given a task such as this who goes willingly to help and do his best. And when you look at the steps taken by him on the ground, all those jobs he did in providing the food, setting up the bakeries, the kitchens, his involvement with the infrastructure, all show a man willing to help. But the important point to note in all of this is that he wasn't sent down there to receive reports of crimes. That was never in his brief. He was sent down there to help. I dare say, the last thing in anyone's mind when he was appointed as the garrison commander and sent down there was that he would be dealing with the reports of crimes being passed to him by international organisations. They're simply no evidence that this was envisaged in any way. And when General Gotovina was spoken to on the 8th of August by General Forand, he said, Any problems you have, General Cermak will help you. And that's the purpose of that role. This Court is now going asked to structure a case against Mr. Cermak of a nature where a part of what he did was not something planned, thought of. It was just something he took upon himself. And in doing that, he took that upon himself, because they came to him. As General Deverell said, when you're of senior rank, it's the usual case in international situations that people go to you with your problem. And that's what was exactly happening to Mr. Cermak. We know that this became far wider and went to the police and went to others. But his handling of these reports and issues was not something that had ever been structured or planned. There's simply no evidence that how he acted was done in furtherance of any criminal plan. Simply not there. When his role was discussed by President Tudjman, again, it wasn't a role that envisaged him receiving information about crimes. That was never part of the brief, how he handled it, he tried his best, and he passed it on to others who had to deal with it. Let us move on now to the next allegation by the Prosecution which attempts to invest Mr. Cermak powers and authority he simply didn't have. And this has been given various titles. Yesterday, by Mr. Carrier, enhanced military status. We've had enhanced authority. We have had extraordinary enhanced authority. So allegation being made that in some way he had far wider powers that he could have used in such a way as to prevent what was happening on the ground in relation to crimes. Well, we know what he did and how he passed it on, which was consistent with his responsibility as a citizen. So if we -- we take that position, which the Court, in my submission, must do. We mustn't think ill of an accused because he is an accused. But you take that position of the very fact he is passing on information and complaining about crimes that have been committed, why, then, if he had this enhanced authority, would he have not have issued it. It's simply a contradiction in what he did do and what he tried to do, and this concept that, somehow, he had extra power and could have done more. If he had, from the evidence we've seen, he would have done more. Now, this extraordinary enhanced authority is a complete construction to try and invest in him a form of criminal liability. I'm going to refer to one exhibit that sums up the lack of authority. We could be here weeks going through it. It's D1016, and it's the request for the authorisation for expenses for a prosciutto ham that was used at a lunch for a delegation. Well, if you can't order a ham sandwich without authority, it beggars belief that you start ordering the police, military police, the armed force in the area if you don't even have that authority to order a ham. It is simply a fiction to have put in this concept into the case and not based it upon solid and reliable evidence. Prosecution, in their discussion in the final brief on the subject of the enhanced authority, make references to numerous passages of evidence that, in fact, cite the opposite of what they intend, and a classic is -- is that in paragraph 334, where they rely on the Defence witness Skare Ozbolt, and they cite transcript 18101. She actually described him as being a landless knight with competence unknown. "He did not know what his area of responsibility was." The witnesses they rely upon are those primarily from the international community who, themselves, did not know what Mr. Cermak's responsibility and authority was, and had no knowledge themselves of the workings of the Croatian military or civil system. All their witnesses said, We don't know what his authority was. And as Mr. Berikoff said, His authority wasn't recognised on the ground. General Forand, exactly the same. Mr. Roberts, exactly the same. So, what do we have here in summary? We have a man put into an ad hoc role to try and help establish, at a time of great pressure for Croatia, the normalisation of life on the ground of a part of their territory that had previously been occupied by rebel forces. His brief was that of a civil nature in its discharge. At one stage, the Prosecution are referring to him having extraordinarily enhanced authority without any citation as to where that authority comes from or any clear definition of what it was. And then, on the other hand, we have them citing the powers of the garrison commander as found in the Croatian armed forces regulations. So two competing areas of authority: One, if you're in that position and you have that power, you have that power; the other being something not defined at all. In their section of their final brief, starting at paragraph 300, Prosecution deal with Mr. Cermak's authority as the garrison commander. They state that he joined the military in August 1995 as an active member. A key proposition for them is to try and establish that he was, if they're relying on the garrison commander regulations, that he was an active member. In fact, we know from the surrounding evidence that the tasks he was given were rather different. And when one looks at the orders and reports, all of which, at the time, refer to his brief of normalisation, in our submission, it is quite clear that he had that role and that task and was not formally carrying out the role of a garrison commander, and that is what he spent his time doing. His tasks were of a non-military nature. However, much time has been spent on the authority of a garrison commander, and the Prosecution, in their final brief analyse in great detail, as we did, as it has been a feature of the case, as to what that authority was. What is staggering in the Prosecution final brief is the utter failure to deal with the conclusions of the expert witnesses, Feldi, Kovacevic, Deverell, and Albiston, on the authority and responsibilities of a garrison commander. Instead, they rely on their own interpretation of the service regulations, which General Feldi was responsible for, and also the 1993 organisational order of work in the garrison. In their final brief, they cite various passages from General Deverell and others as to what the authority of a garrison commander was. In all those citations, in fact, it is the opposite of their proposition that the witness is advancing, and there are clear examples of this. We have a very detailed file on it, and no doubt the Court will be checking those footnotes itself, and I want to go to one in particular which can serve as an example. It's paragraph 309, the end of that paragraph, where the assertion is made that Deverell opined that the expectation of having HV units with potentially separate lines of subordination and command militated in favour of granting adequate authority and powers to the garrison commander to allow him to discharge his responsibility to impose regulations aimed at establishing and maintaining a climate of good order and military discipline. Well, cited is General Deverell's report, Exhibit D1784, pages 23 and 24. And he says quite clearly: "Thus, the garrison commander is responsible for imposing such regulations as are required to achieve this," being the climate of good order and military discipline cited in the text. But this part is not; for example, establish vehicle speed limits, allocate routes within the garrison, determine opening times for facilities, such as fuel and ammunition depots, allot training facilities to units, and regulate the use of accommodation. These facilities will be used by and largely exist for units not organic to the garrison and, therefore, not subordinated to the garrison commander. At the transcript, page 24298 to 300: "The garrison commander can only be responsible for the discipline of those who are subordinated to him." This whole section of the Prosecution final brief has confused subordinates and the right to discipline subordinates with that of general powers of authority. Your Honour, that's 1.46, and I know that that is a break time.

utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, without revealing the identity, that footnote firstly refers to a protected witness in this case who merely stated that his role was not clearly defined in that extract and that he had to refer to Zadar. Nothing more, nothing less. The second reference is to a sheet of corrections by this witness; P88, page 1. Nothing there about submitting himself to Cermak's authority. Your Honours are referred to an organisational chart of the MUP by the Prosecution. Nothing again, in terms of Ivan Cermak.
