utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: My apologies, not question 7, question 5 of the Trial Chamber's questions concerning a table in the Prosecution final brief concerning restrictions of movement. I want to look at the concept of restriction of movement, first of all, because it's rather misleading to say that General Cermak informed the internationals of restrictions of movement, as if he was imposing on them the restrictions. That is a very distinct proposition. Informing them does not mean that you are necessarily imposing the restrictions unless you've made that decision yourself. The example that we would refer to on this is at paragraph 364 of the Prosecution pre-trial -- final brief, where they assert Mr. Cermak restricted movement. They cited the Witness Liborius, that there was restriction of movement, and Cermak was contacted about it. And also, as a result of that contact, he was able to move freely thereafter. That doesn't mean that the blockage that happened on the ground as between Liborius and the ECMM monitors, or in other instances, UNCRO or HRAT officials, was as a result of any imposition by Mr. Cermak which had prevented them progressing on their journey through parts of the area. What it means is that, in fact, they phoned for him to help and sort out their difficulty. Now, if he want going to sort out their difficulty and he wanted to restrict movement so that crimes could be committed, it contradicts the JCE theory of his involvement if he is then in the process of helping, if he can, to secure them a free passage and prevent the local officials from obstructing their journey. The evidence in this case, we submit, and I will deal with that particularly in answer to the Trial Chamber's questions, is that it was the local-level commanders of the MUP, local HV commanders, or even CALOs who were those who imposed the restrictions and blocked movement of internationals on an ad hoc basis. But, in our submission, the evidence in this case shows that, in fact, they were travelling quite freely and regularly and without restriction. And it may well be the case here that the issue on restrictions of movement, as it does in many cases where international bodies face each other, became one of those sores and points that was a continuing spark of controversy, exactly as General Jack Deverell explained when he gave his evidence. The de facto and de jure authority by which General Cermak could restrict movement or could grant freedom of movement has not been established by the evidence in this case. The evidence, in fact, established that he was operating on behalf of decisions made by others and was the person used to communicate that information. Right at the start in Knin, it was a security issue as between the internationals and the Croatian armed forces as to whether, almost directly after liberation of the territory, they were free to move around. Mr. Akashi himself, when he discussed this with Mr. Cermak, acknowledged the difficulties of the security and that freedom of movement that General Forand wanted would be a matter that could be provided when the security of the area had been established. And that's how matters arose right at the start. And the Cermak document that was issued on that date saying they could move in Knin and Drnis and not to go off the main roads, they were advised not to travel there, was providing a piece of paper so that that could be used by them, if necessary, to go through any blockages, check-points, or other areas and give them help and assistance in their work. That was the simple purpose of it. It was not General Cermak sitting in an office and deciding himself where operations were, what was happening, and how he could control matters. As you've been explained to, he simply was not (a), in that position; (b), ever required to do that through the local military structure. But he was passing on what were the valid security concerns after an armed conflict which the local Croatian authorities and the senior Croatian authorities recognised as being potentially dangerous. One must remember they'd taken over land that was their own but they did not know what lay around in the surrounding terrain. This is a very difficult terrain. It is not one which is a network of motorways and roads and places of installations, large towns and villages. It is a wild piece of geography. Within that district, it was perfectly conceivable to those who were in command of the armed forces that there could be rebel groups or others waiting to attack back against their forces. All Cermak did was pass on what was believed to have been the best area for them to travel in for their own safety at the time. Court is reminded the UN restricted their own movement by having a system of grading of the security concerns for the region. Let us now look at the matters that arise from the Question 5 of the Trial Chamber. The chart which the Prosecution has compiled and the footnotes that have been cited in -- in support, in our submission, are unclear and generalised descriptions of what took place and do not describe perpetrators of crimes sufficiently or adequately, and it is necessary to look very carefully at what has been cited to the Court. We will now look at each item by item. The first place, Benkovac town, on 7th to 8th August, where it is recorded that there was looting by Croatian armed forces, the 134th and the 72nd Military Police in Benkovac. Firstly, Benkovac is outside the area of the Knin garrison, and confirmed by Prosecution witnesses as well that General Cermak had no authority at all in Benkovac. And, in our submission, his letter that he had issued on the 8th of August to General Forand had no relevance in relation to the -- to -- to Benkovac as a place. In the footnote at 1312, it's cited an UNMO patrol was stopped at the HV check-point by the military police and the UNMO was, for the second time, banned from entering the town of Benkovac. In our submission, this is not as a result of any order by General Cermak that they were stopped at Benkovac. There is simply no evidence of any operational order, nor could he have issued such an order to forces there, saying, Do not permit internationals into Benkovac at this time and on this day. The events of looting are described by the UNMO personnel who go to that place, and it is the taking of goods. What is of importance at this time, on the 7th to 8th of August, is to note that on the 7th of August, P301, P355, P111, P805, and P2146 show that the internationals were moving around this area without any hindrance. For the 8th of August, also see P806 and P112. It's clear from the reports of the commander of the 3rd Company of the 72nd Military Police that the military police were in Benkovac and were aware of events that were taking place. There is a SIS report dated the 18th of August, D984, pages 2 and 3, which confirms that troops that were known about at that time were dealing with -- were performing in an irresponsible way and committing irresponsible crimes. But this was not sanctioned by the local commanders. This was not something that they supported. This was not something that they wanted to take place. Turning now to the next footnote, the next place in the town, Cetina, on the 12th of August, footnote 1314. It's recorded on the Prosecution table that the village was burned down and looted, and we should look at the footnote to see what is cited, P364, page 3. And the report is that there was a Croatian police in Cetina and that while the village was inspected, they were stopped by that police and this had been a place that was observed by KenBat during the Grahovo offensive. In that report, there's no mention of burning and looting. Furthermore, on that day, other exhibits, P32, P808, P815, P117, D65, show UNMO representatives moving around the area. It is probably the Witness Dangerfield, P699, page 6, who is the source of the evidence concerning Cetina, because in that statement he said, During other patrols we were arrested and escorted out of the sector because we had seen looting and burning in the village of Cetina. The extent of that and what took place isn't specified, and whether the two are connected in the sense of what was happening to him and the events taking place is not made clear. Benkovac, 21st of August, houses burned by the 134th, if we go to the footnote 1315, P403, page 3, where it is stated: "In the area of Benkovac, there are also some restrictions to movement." It is not specified who restricted movement. Other teams are moving around without difficulty at that time and even able to report on crimes that are taking place; D93, P125. Other UNCRO representatives are able to move in the area. D623, D93, P125, P45, P815. At this time, on the 20th of August, D1002, Croatian forces were employed in the area, mopping up the terrain, sorting out -- seeking infiltrated enemy gangs and securing roads and communications. What we submit is this, that what was happening was that at a local level, local commanders of police and local commanders of troops were obstructing the passage of internationals without there being any directive or order from higher authority within the Croatian forces or government.

And in fact, that method was employed throughout Bosnia, as they went through the villages of Bosnia, as they went through other villages, the alleged withdrawal of the JNA, followed by the paramilitaries, TOs, who were JNA in disguise, committing crimes after they had gone. And it was very much a feature of the Serbian tactics in relation to those states that they were -- they were passing through in order to commit crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Before I begin, I would like to just let the Chamber know and all of the parties that I will be talking about command responsibility issues, certain issues relating to artillery and specific crimes relating to General Markac, and Mr. Mikulicic will discuss the armed conflict issue and JCE. Before I begin my presentation, I wanted -- I think it would be remiss of us all, having been here two and a half years, not to thank the court staff, the Court Officer, specifically Mr. Nilsson, the technical staff, all of the legal officers, the court reporter, the guards who treated our clients and us with respect, and the last, but not least, the interpreters for their work because without them we wouldn't be heard. So preliminarily, it's a custom in my jurisdiction to do something like that, and given the fact that we've been together for so long, I think it's appropriate to do. Your Honours, colleagues across the well, and learned Defence counsel, the Office of the Prosecutor's final brief, in our view, contains many misconceptions and a thorough lack of analysis of facts as applied to law, especially regarding General Markac. The OTP's final brief is rife with conclusory leaps and attributions without underlying citation to the record. We've heard some of that from the last day and a half. Overall, what stands out as a rhetorical pattern, recite general facts, allege specific conclusions and legal consequences, and provide no evidence. The same pattern generally has been followed in closing argument. The result is essentially an invitation to this Chamber to commit serious factual and legal error. I trust the Chamber will most definitely not do that. The OTP has failed to demonstrate a connection which the case law requires with respect to General Markac specifically, a nexus between crimes and a specific failure on the part of the commander. At first, I thought the rhetorical pattern was only contained in the brief, but then not after listening to yesterday's prevention. In particular, Mr. Russo, at page 45 of yesterday's argument regarding artillery, cites Zdravko Janic, special police commander, called by the Prosecution. Mr. Russo said Janic "testified that there were no military targets inside the town of Gracac proper." But when one looks at his transcript reference, which is transcript page 6393 to 94, this does not exist. In fact Gracac is never mentioned. If we could show the document, please, with the transcript reference. Janic talks about his own axis of attack which does not include Gracac. The transcript reference -- and I will paraphrase beginning at line 18: "You said that there were predetermined targets. Were there any predetermined targets in civilian populated areas in your line of attack? "A. No, there weren't. Which stage are we talking about, the first stage of Operation Storm or the entire operation?" And then the question is: "Operation Storm, the first stage on the 4th and 5th of August." Mr. Janic continues to describe his line of attack which did not include Gracac. He states: "This was an uninhabited area. There weren't even villages in that area in my line of attack. Further on he is asked what were the predetermined targets, were they soldiers or were there any other military installations or equipment? What were the targets? "The predetermined targets," he answers, "were the enemy positions and the depth of their defence line, the artillery positions their command post, their depots. The targets were the enemy infrastructure that they used to defend their lines. Those were the exclusive targets that we had. Whenever conducting an operation, well, it wasn't possible to have any other targets. All the targets were military targets. The purpose was to breakthrough the enemy defence line and to attain the operation's objectives. It wasn't possible to have any other objectives." He was never asked about Gracac. The attribution is false. Interestingly, in reviewing the 98 bis arguments, Mr. Russo made the same argument and I actually made the same rebuttal. Let's talk about what Mr. Russo ignored during his artillery discussion regarding the special police. He ignored the testimony of Josip Turkalj, a witness called by the Prosecution, the man in charge of special police use of artillery after the initial defence lines were breached. And the transcript references there are 13697, 13703 to 707. In that testimony, Mr. Turkalj discusses that there were 15 rounds of artillery for Gracac. Fifteen. And the accusation that Gracac was excessively shelled holds no water. Turkalj had specific instructions to ensure that civilians would not be in harm's way as far as artillery was concerned and that there were at least three military targets in the town itself. Mr. Russo ignores P102, an UNMO report which, incidentally, reports that 15 shells fell in the area of Gracac on August 4th. And P111, at page 3 which describes main artillery impacts on the main junction in Gracac. This was Croatian artillery pursuing the retreating ARSK forces as described in P108, another UNMO report discussing the ARSK withdrawal of tanks and artillery from Gracac. Mr. Russo also ignored the Prosecution's artillery expert, Lieutenant-Colonel Konings. He had no opinions critical of the special police's use of artillery in Operation Storm. The Prosecution never even asked him whether he should review the use of artillery in Operation Storm by the special police, including targeting issues. That's at transcript reference 14775 to 76. Finally, Mr. Russo ignores page 21 of P401, which Mr. Kehoe discussed, that said General Forand referring to the Croatian military's use of artillery said it was excellent. Mr. Tieger in his opening statement described the special police as "from the virtual outset of entering towns and villages, the special police began committing crimes." We had discussed this many times in our presentation of our Defence, in our 98 bis arguments and in our briefing. Guilt by proximity. Let's look at what -- where perhaps Mr. Tieger may have gotten this. Let's look at General Leslie's interview, D329, page 3. First of all -- if we go up a little bit, I'm sorry. The first reference is on page 2, again with respect to artillery. The transcript of this interview describes General Leslie talking about how he is a professional about artillery and he can comment it with some degree of validity. He says at the second-last sentence: "It killed a lot of civilians and we'll never know the exact number but estimates -- estimates range from 10 to 25.000 dead." And we all know that that's completely false. As a matter of fact it's a lie. If we go to page 3, Mr. Leslie -- General Leslie again talks about the special police at a time when he wasn't even in Sector South. "There were a variety of organisations that then swept into the former Serbian Krajina. They were special police teams, wearing their very distinctive blue uniforms, who were engaging [sic] in hunting and killing in the mountains of Serbian civilians. And I saw dozens and dozens of farm houses and even villages burning, many, many days, in some cases months, after the initial assault had taken place." Again, blue uniforms identifying special police in the Serbian Krajina. Not anywhere specifically. Again, complete fabrication. Special police did not wear blue uniforms. Special police were not engaged in hunting and killing in the mountains of Serb civilians. I would now like to go through certain portions of the Prosecution's brief. Paragraph 387, the first sentence here is particularly galling and brazen. It says that: "Markac ordered persecution ..." And if we go further into that second line: "... and, in relation to Grubori, murder." There is no citation, factual basis for that comment. None. Think about that for a minute. The Prosecution would have you believe that General Markac ordered, in relation to Grubori, murder. There's no exhibit reference. No transcript reference. Nothing. In that same paragraph, the OTP again states as fact and without attribution: "... Markac was aware that his forces were engaged in criminal conduct against the Serbian community." No cite, no exhibit number, no transcript reference. Other references, paragraph 386 of the Prosecution's brief states that: "... Markac reported false information regarding his subordinates' crimes and suppressed their investigation ..." This is an severely misleading characterisation of the evidence the Court has heard. The omission of the legal standard here is striking. Superiors are entitled, even expected, to rely on information provided by subordinates. More importantly, the relevant period for evaluating the reasonableness of reliance on reports is the time they were provided and subsequently forwarded to higher units. The Nuremburg Rendulic Rule clearly reflects a rejection of hindsight as a standard of judgement. In the case of the United States v. List, otherwise known as the Control Council 10 case out of Nuremburg, the court there succinctly stated the standard, which is well-established customary international law, by which a commander is to be judged without hindsight. And I will quote from pages 1296 and 976 that decision. "We are obliged to judge the situation as it appeared to the defendant at the time. If the facts were such as would justify action by the exercise of judgement after giving consideration to all the factors and existing possibilities, even though the conclusion reached may have been faulty, it cannot be said to be criminal." General Markac forwarded all the reports later alleged to have been false in the midst of high operational tempo and when information was thin. The record includes at least two attempts by General Markac to ensure that his superior at the time, the HV General Staff, had the most current and accurate information that he had. Those being P575 and P576. The two reports on the Plavno operation of August 25th, 1995. The information in those reports was provided by him, to him, by subordinates, subordinates who, based on all his past experience, he had no reason to believe were wrong, were lying, or were misleading him. When General Markac ordered the Lucko commander, Mr. Turkalj to get written reports from the group leaders related to Grubori on September 1st, 1995, a reasonable measure, those reports all stated that armed conflict occurred in Grubori on the 25th. What was the use for him to conduct any further administrative questioning? There is no evidence that any single person told or reported to General Markac that what happened in Grubori was, in fact, a crime. Paragraph 389. Here we found highly suggestive by characteristically unspecific references to criminal conduct. The most troubling is the truly silly allegation of mens rea grounded on knowledge that elderly persons were present in an area of operations. Exactly what additional duty did the presence of elderly persons impose on Markac under the OTP's theory? If we look at paragraph 391: "... Markac was aware of the substantial likelihood that murder would be committed in the execution of his plans for the Grubori operation." If we scroll down to the footnote, please. Two cases are cited for this. How is that evidence? Paragraph 391 [sic]. Here the Prosecution alleges Markac prompted the special police "to commit crimes ... in relation to Grubori." Further, the OTP alleges failure to take reasonable and necessary measures to prevent and punish crimes by his forces, "thereby creating a climate of impunity." This passage is truly representative of the modus operandi of the brief that I mentioned above. This paragraph conflates issuing orders for lawful military operations with specifically intending unlawful acts. It is missing precisely what the law requires, a connection between crimes and a specific failure on the part of the commander. The conclusions the OTP has asked -- asked the Court to draw from these generalised facts are entirely unsupported. The OTP never tells us what necessary or reasonable measures General Markac was supposed to take, just that he didn't take them. Why? Because they know from their own witness, state prosecutor Zeljko Zganjer, that the only entity that could deal with murder and other serious crimes was the crime police, not the special police. And this is transcript reference 11609 to 10. Paragraph 395. The Prosecution says: "Markac was physically present on the scene of ... crimes committed by his subordinates ..." This is another misleading suggestion attempting a connection between a very general statement and criminal responsibility. This passage suggests Markac's presence at the scene of crimes and is -- because of that he is therefore criminally liable. The invitation to error is to conclude that Markac was physically present at crimes and actually declined opportunities to personally interrupt acts of criminal violence. It is no wonder that this paragraph includes no citation to two and a half of evidence, and also no wonder the allegation isn't elaborated in later sections of the brief. The OTP spends a scant three paragraphs on superior responsibility with not one citation to the appropriate case law. Regarding its discussion of superior liability, the OTP's neglect of the evidence before the Court is striking. Despite detailed evidence presented to this Court concerning the actual extent of General Markac's authority within the MUP, here the OTP relates his authority in the most general terms. This characterisation, of course, better suits their urging of his culpability based on his position rather than his conduct. This is a gross departure from the legal standard of superior responsibility. Paragraph 398 is an allegation of actual notice of crimes without citation to authority. Even so, it recites a simplified account of a superior's duties with respect to knowledge of crimes. Here they would have this Court understand that leaders have no option other than to punish. This passage conveniently neglects widely recognised legal effect of reporting of offensives to responsible authorities. Moreover, not one single mention is made of the general MUP, media, and NGO awareness of the events in question. Everyone from Minister of the Interior Jarnjak, to Josko Moric, to Stjepan Buhin, to Ivan Cetina, to Zeljko Sacic, to Witness 86 and Witness 84 are alleged to have been advised about Grubori. Yet Markac is the one who is alleged to be criminally responsible for it despite the fact that it is the crime police that is responsible to conduct these criminal investigations. Another crucially misleading characterisation of Markac's authority is brought forth in paragraph 403, relating to "assisting criminal police in investigation when necessary." This argument is dealt with in Markac Defence brief paragraphs 133 to 93 so I won't go into that in detail. But, as I've stated earlier, criminal offences, their investigation, the power is vested in the criminal police sector of MUP. D527, Article 17. The Prosecutor knows all too well the significance of this suggestion especially in light of the Boskoski decision, where the conduct alleged there including murder, grave violence and destruction of homes and property were criminal offences which the Trial Chamber there found could not be adequately handled internally by the Ministry of Interior as an internal disciplinary breach. And I cite that Trial Chamber decision at 521. I think it is important for the Chamber to hear specifics about the Boskoski Trial Judgement and Appeals Judgement because it is so similar to the case that we are dealing with, with respect to General Markac. And I'm talking about specifically paragraphs 523 to 526 of the Trial Judgement. The evidence presented indicate -- in the Boskoski case that he was present as minister of interior for over an hour at a house while ten ethnic Albanians were being held there, guarded by police. The prisoners were lying face down with their heads covered. Boskoski was told they were terrorists who had been captured. While he was in the village, he heard firing and could see houses burning. Even the Chamber in that case established from the evidence presented that the men being held had been severely beaten prior to the time Boskoski had seen them, they could not conclude from the evidence that Boskoski witnessed any mistreatment or "should have deduced from the appearance of the ten that there had been criminal mistreatment." Similarly, even though homes were burning, the Chamber concluded that no evidence presented proved that Boskoski should have known that there was arson or wanton destruction of property. The Chamber found that he had been supplied an explanation by the police that there had been an armed conflict between the security forces and terrorists, coupled with the testimony that he had been shown three fire-arms and ammunition that he was told were seized from the terrorist, and that was sufficient to support Boskoski's understanding of the events. The Trial Chamber found no evidence that Boskoski saw or was told of any person being shot or killed while visiting the village. In affirming the acquittal, the Appeals Chamber stated that the information in possession of the civilian police was determined in the ordinary course to have led an investigative judge and the public prosecutor to conduct a proper investigation as anticipated by the law in such circumstances. Though evidence presented did not confirm that Boskoski had ordered the notification to the criminal police, the record indicated that members of police officers in his ministry passed the relevant information on to competent authorities. That's at paragraph 267. The similarity between the Boskoski case and the case facing General Markac is striking. One important difference, General Markac was never in Grubori. General Markac never saw with his own eyes what happened there. General Markac learned everything about Grubori from written reports from subordinates who were either on the scene or who had participated in the action. Those written reports talked about armed conflict. Let's look at reasonableness from General Markac's standpoint with respect to Grubori. He gets notice the evening of August 25th that something happened in an area where his forces were operating. He sends his Chief of Staff, Zeljko Sacic, to find out more information the same day he gets this information. The next day, his Chief of Staff sets out for Knin and he finds out from his Chief of Staff that there are dead bodies and that there are police on the scene. Now if a crime occurred, it is the competence of the MUP criminal police to investigate it. If the deaths were not, in fact, the result of lawful armed conflict, they had a legal obligation to investigate. All the information in General Markac's possession is relayed to him by others. Even Boskoski who was on the scene seeing the burning is not held criminally responsible for failing to act. Unless General Markac has information which has been provided to him which is to the contrary, there is no reason for him not to believe what he has learned from his subordinates. In addition, Witness 86 and Witness Buhin were waiting for instructions from Ivica Cetina, the head of the Zadar crime police, under whose jurisdiction any criminal investigation fell. This is Witness 86's testimony at transcript 5292. Paragraph 433 of the Prosecution's brief. Even where the Prosecutor admits that Markac initiated investigative efforts commensurate with his resources and authority, the Prosecutor attributes ungrounded, nefarious motives to these efforts. Paragraph 434 alleges that Markac had a discussion with Cermak about what Cermak would say to UNTV. This is undocumented, unsubstantiated and non-existent. There is no factual reference that General Markac talked to General Cermak about anything related to Grubori other than the initial notice that something happened on August 25th. This is an effort to construct an agreement between Cermak and Markac to mislead regarding the events of the day. Paragraph 439. Almost every act in this paragraph is alleged to be independent of anything Markac did. This and subsequent paragraphs paint the picture that Zeljko Sacic could sow fear and independently wield enough influence to cow Witnesses 84, 86, an entire office of police authorities, as well as Cermak, Moric, Jarnjak, Cetina, and Buhin. Paragraphs 442 and 443. At this point in the brief, as to Markac's own actions, it appears the Prosecutor would have it both ways. In this unbelievable account, he has failed to personally intervene and criminally absented himself from supervising his subordinates while simultaneously encouraging and soliciting them to commit crimes while present at the scene of the events. It ignores the reality that the undisputed evidence is from August 8th to the 21st, the special police were not operating in Sector South beyond their remit. It is difficult to conjure a vision of command more divorced from the realities and challenges of combat leadership. This discussion completely ignores the chain of command and merely equates Markac's position as being an impetus for culpability. In essence, the argument both in the brief and during oral argument is that a unit of the special police went into Grubori on August 25th, 1995, in a mop-up operation, and following Markac's orders, murdered five civilians. Markac knew that the Lucko Unit was involved. He knew that some or all of its members committed murder and he didn't punish them for it. He then covered it up, and he knew it all by 5.00 in the evening on August 25th, 1995. That's the Prosecution's view. That's the simple view. In my opinion, that's the warped view, the completely wrong view, which leads to conclusions justified by unsubstantiated assumptions. Justice is supposed to be blind but this method of argument by the OTP is an attempt to circumvent justice. Markac is presumed to have criminal culpability through conclusory statements without an analysis of the evidence as applied to the law. Prosecution has argued throughout this case that internal -- the internal control department is a means of discipline for the special police. It's wrong. I'll refer you to Janic's trial testimony, 6199 to 200, where he discusses that they did intelligence analysis and security assessments, among other things. General Markac can act on information that is only as good as the source, and the source for his information are his subordinates. To be blunt, if he is being lied to, misled, misinformed, deliberately or due to the incompetence or human failings of others, he cannot be blamed for passing on information that he gets from those who were either on the ground, asked to look into the matter, or who didn't have the guts to tell the truth back in 1995. The multiple investigations undertaken by the Croatian state attorney's office in Grubori, one in 2001 by Mr. Zeljko Zganjer and the second one which is still ongoing by Mladen Bajic, right at the Markac Defence was in the middle of its case in-chief, have done nothing to clarify what happened there. But significantly have not produced any evidence that, at the time of the events, General Markac knew that members of the special police committed murder of civilians on August 25, 1995. Zganjer said that he found no evidence, in 2001, that General Markac had gone anything to cover up the events in Grubori, nor that he either influenced anyone else during the relevant time-period. If he had, he would have been obligated to pursue charges. That's what he said himself at transcript reference 11609 to 11. The Prosecution talks a lot about P505, the alleged Markac reply to the Elisabeth Rehn inquiry into Grubori. The Prosecutor states in its brief that Zganjer found P505 to be "authentic." But that's not the whole story. The OTP has not told you what it did not cite in footnote 1689 that was discussed in transcript references 11617 to 11619. That being Zganjer's testimony that he did not know P505 never came to Minister Jarnjak or left the Ministry of Interior to go to Ms. Rehn until it was raised in cross-examination by my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic. "Had I been aware of the information at the time, I would have called into question what I thought." He was presented with D909 and D910, a memo which had requested the registry log-book to determine whether or not the letter was actually drafted or sent. P505 uses the -- used by the OTP as "evidence" of a cover-up is weak. It is unsigned, has no stamp, has no number. But what better person to ask if P505 was a response to her inquiries than Ms. Rehn herself. The Office of the Prosecutor brought her here to testify but failed to adduce any evidence that she ever received it. I want to address the climate of impunity argument. The Office of the Prosecutor discusses that General Markac's alleged knowledge of crimes committed in Grubori on August 25th, prior to the Lucko Unit going to Ramljane on August 26th, was evidence of "impunity and failure to punish." This is a false argument. It is a straw man, and I will tell you why. It simply wasn't possible. The August 26th freedom train security operation in the vicinity of Ramljane was set up prior to the Plavno operation via orders of August 23rd, which are D563 and D739. The Lucko Unit alone was set up to operate to provide security for the Freedom train. It was to handle, as we've heard, the most sensitive part of the rail line. Now, P190 is a map. I'm not going to pull it up but Ramljane is past Knin on the way to Split. Grubori is 40 to 45 minutes north of Knin. So we can keep in mind on the map where those locations are. Knin in between Grubori to the north, Ramljane to the south. Now, the knowledge, so-called, that has been imputed to -- by the OTP to General Markac that Lucko, itself, was a unit that was through Grubori on the 25th and had committed crimes there, assumes that Lucko was the only special police unit to take part in mop-up operations on the 25th in the Plavno valley. Well, there were almost 600 members of the special police participating in this operation. Not one witness has testified, not one, that it was known to General Markac, his subordinates, the fundamental police of Knin, or any of the internationals, on August 25th, on or before the Freedom train operation on August 26th, that Lucko specifically was the unit that went through Grubori on the 25th. Lucko was one of six units of 580 special police members involved on August 25th in Plavno where Grubori was located. These units were the Sisak-Moslavina, Zagreb, Brod-Posavina, Split-Dalmatia, Lucko, and Osijek Baranja. When Markac was told late on 25th that something happened in Grubori, what evidence exists that, first, he knew where Grubori was, or, second, he knew that it was the Lucko Unit? None. No one identified the unit, nor is there any evidence that General Markac knew which unit went through Grubori on the evening of August 25th. As far as Markac knew, the reports from the field from all six units were that nothing happened. And that is essentially what P575 says. The word "Grubori" appears nowhere in P575. This is the first report General Markac sends to the Main Staff. We must focus on General Markac's state of mind on August 25th, when he is told something happened in Grubori. This wasn't the Grubori mop-up operation. This was the Plavno mop-up operation. Can I go into private session for a moment please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Registrar. The argument that sending the Lucko Unit into the freedom train operation on August 26th after General Markac learned that "something happened" on the evening of August 27th somehow is evidence that General Markac allowed Lucko to operate with impunity, and is an example of a failure to punish special police members for crimes is simply wrong based upon the Prosecution's own evidence. utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted to get back to the issue of notice for just a moment to General Markac. Notice, Prosecution would equate notice to General Markac of crimes by supposedly driving down a road and seeing someone who was dead and automatically equating that with crimes committed by the special police. I wanted to just briefly touch upon one issue which relates to questions asked about the transcript in Brioni and General Markac and his suggestion of accusing the Serbs of having launched a sabotage attack against Croatian forces referred to in the Brioni transcript. There's been some questioning regarding this issue as some sort of either criminal intent or character flaw or -- I don't know what. Even though this pretext for attack never occurred, under Article 372 of the Additional Protocol I of the Geneva Convention, this is a legitimate ruse of war. Feigning provocation is not an illegitimate ruse described in the protocol. Decoys, mock operations, misinformation which are intended to mislead the adversary or induce him to act recklessly do not infringe rules of international law applicable in an armed conflict and are not perfidious. That is, again, Article 37(2) of the Additional Protocol. I want to talk in some detail about Mr. Celic. He is heavily relied upon by the Prosecution and his credibility on the issue regarding Grubori. And I want to go through as much of his testimony as possible to -- to really stress what I believe to be the lack of credibility of Mr. Celic. Transcript references here are page 7956 to 57, in relation to Grubori. We know who Celic is. He was a person who initially wrote that nothing happened in Grubori and later claimed that Mr. Sacic dictated a report to him to say that something happened in Grubori. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "I believe that things were the way he," meaning Sacic, "had put them. Not at any moment did I doubt what he was saying," Celic testified. When Your Honour Judge Orie confronted Celic with the fact that the report's version of events was at odds with his current version of events, Celic responded that the action as described in P564 could have agreed with the experience of another special police unit in the area. When he was again reminded that P564 was written by him and related to his unit, he eventually admitted that the information in the report that was dictated to him was incorrect. That's transcript reference 7957. He failed to provide the Trial Chamber with any reasonable explanation for his failure to bring this to his superior's attention, meaning Turkalj. Because Turkalj was the head of the Lucko Unit and was Celic's superior. Lack of credibility. Transcript reference 8111 to 8112. Under cross-examination, Celic stated that he told Sacic that: "Nothing had happened, that there had been no incident, no prisoner of war, nothing." Celic was then asked: "So you signed a report where you essentially could not confirm the information that was in it?" Celic's answer was: "Absolutely." Again, lack of credibility. When asked if it had crossed his mind, at 8112 to 8113, when he was speaking with Sacic, to ask Sacic who told him what happened in Grubori, Celic testified that he told Sacic to ask the group leaders what had happened. When asked whether Celic himself had asked his section commanders what had happened in Grubori, Celic said no. His lack of initiative is highly suspect. Again, lack of credibility with respect to Celic. 8113 to 1816. Celic was asked: "Bearing in mind that what Mr. Sacic had dictated to you was a fairly dramatic and worrying report, did you not feel, as a junior commander, that you should call these men," meaning Celic's subordinates, "back from leave and establish the facts of what had happened in Grubori?" Celic responded: "From the point when I had the meeting with Sacic, there was no one I could talk to because the men were on leave, because I only went to Zagreb for one day. I spent the night there and then I returned." Again, lack of credibility. P761 at page 41, which is Sacic's -- Celic's interview. I think I need to go into private session for this, Your Honour.
