utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Celic's evidence vis-a-vis what was discussed in the private session is further discredited by the fact that at 0900 hours on the 26th of August he was in Ramljane carrying out an operation. In live testimony, at transcript reference 8026, Celic distanced himself from his initial account stating that he produced his second Grubori report in Gracac after the Ramljane operation. Again, lack of credibility. Transcript reference 7970 to 7971. Balunovic submitted a report, P572. Balunovic was one of the group leaders in Grubori that the Chamber called to testify. This report was starkly at odds with the version of events Balunovic had told Celic because he had reported orally to Celic, his operational commander, that nothing had happened. When Celic was asked whether he had discussed this discrepancy with Balunovic, he testified that he had not done so. He hypothesised that Balunovic's new report might have based on his second report, which is P564, meaning the seconds report written by Celic, which was allegedly dictated to him by Sacic. "Balunovic must have seen it," Celic testified. However, when asked whether he could provide the Chamber with any evidence of Balunovic having read the dictated report, all he could say was: "The report was on the table for everybody to see." The fact that Balunovic was one of Celic's good friends, which is indicated in transcript reference 7967, casts significant doubt on the assertion that he never discussed the striking discrepancy between Balunovic's two reports with Celic. Again, lack of credibility. Transcript 8101 to 8103. When Celic read Balunovic's second report, P572, he failed to discuss the discrepancies between it and Balunovic's first report with Balunovic. The second report contained new information which was not in the report which was dictated to Celic by Sacic, allegedly. Though Celic read Balunovic's report and must have understood that it was alarmingly at odds with Balunovic's initial report, Celic testified that he did not discuss the matter in any detail with Balunovic. This is in spite of the fact that Celic testified he was "surprised and interested" by the additional information contained in Balunovic's report. Again, another lack of credibility. Transcript reference 8098 to 99. When confronted with Flynn's testimony that he saw a huge plume of smoke over Grubori on the afternoon of 25 of August, 1995, and that virtually every structure in the hill-side town was on flames, transcript reference for Flynn is 1064, Celic testified that from a vantage that was approximately a kilometre away from Grubori, on the same day, at roughly the same time, he saw nothing. Again, lack of credibility. Transcript reference 8106 to 8107. Following the operation in Grubori on the 25th, Celic and his fellow special police returned to Gracac in convoy, five per vehicle. When asked whether he had discussed the operation on the way back to Gracac, Celic stated that neither he nor anyone else in the vehicle had discussed the operations. Again, a lack of credibility. Transcript reference 8107 to 8110. When asked whether in line with protocol as a junior commander with the special police, he was obliged to seek information from his section leaders on the amount of ammunition that had been expended on the operation, he conducted an ammunition check -- he was supposed to have conducted an ammunition check at the end of the Grubori operation and he conveniently did not. Transcript reference 8128 to 8129. On page 424 of P762, when describing the events of 26th of August, Celic does not mention having been involved in a meeting with Sacic and Cermak. This description of the day's events contradicts what Celic gave to the Trial Chamber in his live evidence. In court, Celic suddenly remembered that in fact he did have a meeting with Sacic and Cermak, during the course of which Celic had discussed the details of the Grubori operation. It is crystal clear that Celic was a witness who said anything to cast blame on others and not himself. He talked with no one, he saw nothing, he heard nothing, yet he signs reports which went up the chain to General Markac which he knew were false. He accused Sacic of dictating the reports to him, but he failed to confront his own subordinates for writing false reports, nor did he tell his own commander, Turkalj, of this occurrence. With respect to planning and Markac's alleged involvement in planning of Operation Storm, I refer the Chamber to two exhibits, D535 and D543. Those are orders from the HV Main Staff dated June 26th, 1995, and July 29th, 1995, which spelled out the operation to be carried out in two stages over three days from the Velebits to the Gospic-Gracac road. Both of those orders, with the plans, were given to Markac. He had no involvement in the planning of those or in terms of planning of Operation Storm. He was given a ready-made plan to implement, not asked to put a plan together. With respect to Donji Lapac, P586, the report of Branislav Bole, which describes Janic's attempt to get the commander of the 118th Regiment to stop burning buildings, and reported that the special police had nothing to do with the burning of Donji Lapac as the special police was outside of Donji Lapac toward Kulen Vakuf. D556 is the report of Janic regarding the same issue, which, as a opposed to the final trial brief at paragraph 411, asserts that Markac ordered the special police artillery to fire on the town of Donji Lapac. D55, page 47, shows the Main Staff log in where Markac contacted the Main Staff at 2120 on the 7th of August. Witness Pavlovic described a heated conversation that General Markac had with General Miljavac from the Main Staff. D555. This contact was from Gracac as there was no way to contact the Main Staff from Lapac. That's transcript reference 25272 to 73. Pavlovic also discussed the special police entry into Donji Lapac after General Markac had prohibited his advance force to open fire on a mixed column of ARSK soldiers and civilians and tanks with heavy weaponry. That's at transcript reference 25259. The last thing I want to talk about, Your Honours, is Gracac. And in brief, I want to refer you to the statement of Mr. Vanderostyne, who is really the sole witness, essentially, that the Prosecution relies on for Gracac. His statement is fairly long. To be frank, it reads like a John le Carre spy novel. But he discusses what he saw in paragraphs 29 and 30. He says in paragraph 29, In the outskirts of Gracac we saw police cars and policemen that were looting. They wore grey uniforms. As we know the special police uniforms are not grey. Either Mr. Vanderostyne is colour-blind or he was guessing. Or he was wrong. What's interesting is, in paragraph 30, he wanted to know whether they should drive back or go to Knin. He asked himself that question. He says, Finally we drove back although we were very scared. We parked in the central square of Gracac. And I just wanted to leave with you the very scared Mr. Vanderostyne, P325. There is the scared Mr. Vanderostyne walking around in Gracac, observing the special police who apparently were looting trees or whatever they were doing, standing there in Gracac. Finally, I wanted to leave you with one thing before I hand it over to my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic. Thomas Jefferson once observed that the tree of liberty must be fertilised by the blood of patriots. General Markac is a patriot. He is a man of integrity and of character, and after years of occupation led the special police honourably and with distinction. And with that I will turn it over to my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: With the permission of the Court, I will give my final speech in Croatian, which is more convenient. Thank you. [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friends, all participants in the proceedings inside the courtroom and outside the courtroom. Da mihi facta, dabo tibi ius. That is what, in the times of antiquity, judges said to the parties in court. My learned friends before me drew your attention to the facts established in these proceedings. Of course, I accept the analysis of the facts presented by my colleagues who spoke before me, especially in relation to JCE, expulsions, shelling, looting, arson, persecution. And from that point of view, I invoke beneficium cohesionis. Your Honours, I would like to call some legal matters that I believe are important for reaching a fair and just decision in these proceedings. As His Honour Judge Schomburg says, there is no truth without justice or justice without truth. The facts are the truth, and justice is the law. Yesterday, on page 24 of the transcript, line 24, the Prosecutor said that the law is clear, and no attempt is further made to elaborate on that assertion. I claim that the law referred to by the Prosecutor is not clear. The Defence is going to show that the -- that law provides a different foundation for having this Court reach a just decision. I'm going to be dealing with two elements. That is, armed conflict and joint criminal enterprise. In this specific case, all crimes charged in the indictment are placed in a specific area, that is, Sector South, at a specific time, that is to say, the period from the month of July until the 30th of September, 1995. The Prosecutor alleges that throughout that period of time in that area a state of armed conflict prevailed. This assertion maid by the Prosecutor actually justifies, in legal terms, the qualification of the alleged crimes in accordance with Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal, because if the context of the incriminations was not an armed conflict, then this Tribunal would not have jurisdiction. Rather, it would only be national courts that would have jurisdiction. That is to say, the judiciary of the Republic of Croatia. It is not in dispute that one of the sources of law of this Tribunal is undisputed customary international law. This source of law and jurisprudence defines the concept of armed conflict, which is in conditio sine qua non of the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. On the basis of the results of the evidence adduced, the Defence asserts that the Prosecutor did not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that in the territory encompassed by the indictment, there was a state of armed conflict after the 8th of August, 1995; that is to say, once Operation Storm was over. Customary international law defines a state of armed conflict in such a way that two legally and factually criteria have to be met to characterise a conflict as an armed conflict, either internal or international. That is to say, the intensity of the conflict, that there has to be protracted armed violence and the level of organisation of the participants in the conflict. In his final brief the Defence indicated relevant sources of law that established the undisputed authorities and precedents that embraced such a characterisation according to the principles established -- establishing the facts from case to case. Final brief, paragraphs 12 through 37. The Defence claims that the evidence adduced undeniably established that the entire political and military leadership of the so-called RSK had left Sector South, the theatre of operations dealt with the indictment. And the evidence indicated by the Defence in its final brief in paragraphs 38 through 41 leads to that conclusion. As the military and political leadership as well as the bulk of the military units of the so-called ARSK had left, intensive combat operations ceased, as did any kind of organisation of the enemy armed forces. Immediately after the operations were halted, and I'm referring to the police specifically, took over its obligations in the liberated territory. I do not know of any example in recent history, if we were to accept the thesis that there is still an armed conflict, that civilian authority would take over its legally established authority in an area where there is still an armed conflict. However, it is correct that in the area of Sector South, in barely accessible mountainous regions, a small number of former members of the so-called ARSK had stayed behind and that they carried out individual and sporadic armed attacks against police forces and the civilians population in the area. However, by no means can these activities be defined as intensive or organised. The repression apparatus of the Republic of Croatia carried out activities aimed at locating and neutralising such groups during daily searches of the terrain that followed after military operation Storm. They were aimed at located and neutralising leftover weaponry, mines and explosive devices, with the basic objective of establishing civilian authority and general safety and security in the liberated area. Such sporadic and unorganised activities of the members of the former so-called ARSK cannot legally be characterised as an armed conflict. Customary international law characterises such as activity as internal disturbances and tensions. By its essence, form and intention, this activity is actually a typical example of terrorist activity. It is the fundamental obligation of every sovereign state to use legal and repressive means against illegal activity, that is, directed at threatening the legal, state and social system of the state concerned. On the basis of the Law on the Interior that was in force at the time of these incidents, the basic function of the special police is combatting terrorism. Therefore, the use of special police in actions of searching the terrain was not only the obligation of the sovereign state to establish law and order in its territory, in order to find and neutralise those who do not accept the legal system of that state, it was their legal obligation as such. There are different examples in contemporary history that were never characterised as that -- as that kind of activity. I would like to remind you of the military and police actions of the Israeli army and police against the members of Hamas, actions of the British army and police against members of the IRA, actions of the Spanish police and army against the members of ETA and so on. As a matter of fact, in these cases they even had a rather good hierarchical organisation, and in some cases they even controlled parts of that territory. That is to say, that there were some elements that could meet the criteria of customary international law that are applied for defining armed conflict. However, that never happened, and no international court ever established jurisdiction, and the jurisdiction of national courts was never brought into question. The evidence adduced, paragraph 38 of our final brief, shows -- that already on the 7th of August, 1995, at the 295th session of the Croatian government, Minister Susak announced the process of demobilisation in the Croatian Army. Thereby, already on the 9th of August that process started and 70.000 members of the Croatian Army were demobilised. This fact leads to the conclusion that the need for military operations to be carried out by the Croatian Army had ceased to exist due to the absence of enemy combat activities of a higher degree of intensity and organisation. The Prosecutor recalls the decision made in the Tadic case in this Tribunal. Namely, that a state of armed conflict ceases to exist once a peace agreement is concluded. The Defence believes that this decision is not applicable in this specific case. First of all, because in accordance with customary international law, peace agreement is just one of the ways in which an armed conflict is brought to an end. Other ways are the factual cessation of hostilities, the establishment of friendly relations, unconditional surrender, or so-called subjugatio, that is to say, subjugation. Additional Protocol I also envisages that the cessation of active hostilities or a general stop in military operations has to exist. The armed conflict in the Republic of Croatia, in this specific case, did not start with a formal declaration of any kind. We know that international law does not require a formal declaration of war in order for a war or armed conflict to start. However, in order to define a state of armed conflict, why would we require a formal document establishing the end of that conflict. Just as the conflict started via facti by an attack of the so-called Army of the Republic of the Serb Krajina against government authorities of Croatia, that is to say, police stations, the conflict ended in the same way, via facti, when the combat activity of the enemy side subsided and when their structures fell apart. I would like to remind Your Honours of examples from recent history in which armed conflicts or, rather, the process of hostilities also ended without any kind of formal agreement. I'm giving the example of the Falklands armed conflict and the war between Iran and Iraq. So, Your Honours, it is the position of the Defence that roughly after the 8th of August, 1995, there was no armed conflict, and that is how it is defined by undisputed international law. This Tribunal actually has no jurisdiction, jurisdictio ratione materiae, to prosecute crimes that were committed upon the conclusion of military operations during military Operation Storm which the Prosecutor charged as the commission of crimes from Articles 3 and 5 from the Statute of this Tribunal. Now I would like to say a few words about joint criminal enterprise. On 29th of May, 2009, I spoke in this courtroom before this Trial Chamber at the beginning of the Defence case and I said that the Defence would prove, contrary to the Prosecutor's allegations, that there could be no question about the existence of a joint criminal enterprise which had allegedly involved my client, General Markac, among other persons. Today, 15 months later, I'm absolutely convinced that Defence has managed to prove its case, i.e., that the Prosecutor has failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that a joint criminal enterprise ever existed and that my client was one of its participants, and that there are legal presumptions to apply the doctrine of the extended JCE category 3. I said then that the style and form of the indictment, in terms of its architecture, reminded me of indictments which had been widely applied in our domestic jurisdiction against perpetrators of alleged crimes against the socialist order of the former state pursuant to Article 26 of the former penal code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Those crimes were allegedly motivated by a joint criminal plan to overthrow the socialist order of the former state. Crimes within that context that may have arisen from that plan were imputed to all the accused. All the states of the former socialist order recognised a similar system. After the fall of the Berlin Wall and transition of political and legal systems, that system simply collapsed because it was rigid and unjust and it was not sustainable because it had existed on the margins of the achievements of modern civilisation and the judicature of the modern civil society of the 20th century. However, despite the opinion of the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic case about an astonishingly similarity between the institute of joint criminal enterprise and the provision of the former penal code of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, Article 26, dealing with the liability of an organiser of a criminal association or organisation, one should clearly point out that this is simply not true. There are three crucial differences between the legal construct of JCE as proffered by the Prosecutor, and Article 26 of the former criminal code of the SFRY. Pursuant to Article 26, the only person who was held liable was the organiser of a criminal association who was also the criminal figure. When it comes to the extended JCE, it is not only the organiser or the leader of an enterprise who is held liable but also potentially all persons by whom the plan has been adopted. Ultimately, this means that the Prosecutor of this Tribunal may indict anybody they consider to be a subscriber to a criminal plan. And in the relevant indictment we can see that these may include various known and unknown individuals. The second difference pursuant to Article 26 lies in the fact that the organiser of a criminal association was held liable only for those crimes which had been committed within the framework of the criminal association's plan and not for the transgressions of its members. An organiser who did not participate in the commission of a crime could have been held responsible only if that act had been envisaged by the plan, and this corresponds with the fundamental form of JCE category 1, but certainly not to its extended form, according to which an accused is held responsible even for crimes that he could only foresee. In that, the character of foreseeability has been objectivised and fails to take into account the subjective traits of each and every accused or the objective circumstances of the context which existed tempore acti at the time when the crime was committed. The task of the Prosecutor in a socialist legal system was nevertheless more challenging and demanding than the task of the Prosecutor at this Tribunal. The former had to establish or, rather, identify a direct perpetrator and subsequently a causal link, or a nexus causalis, between a perpetrator of a crime and the alleged planner or a superiorly positioned member of the alleged criminal plan. In our example in the category 3 of JCE, the Prosecutor does not even deduce evidence to prove that link so that the responsibility of a perpetrator behind a perpetrator is presumed by the foreseeability of the consequence. Needless to say, such a procedural and legal situation is particularly conducive to the work of the Prosecutor and greatly facilitates his procedural duties; whereas, on the other hand, it is particularly prejudicial for the accused because his guilt is actually presumed and equalised with the objective responsibility which, in legal terms, exists only in some civil law cases in connection with the use of the so-called hazardous substance and it is not in criminal law cases. The accused seems to be in a position where he must prove his innocence instead of the Prosecutor having to prove the former's guilt. Such a procedural situation derogates the presumption of innocence. Allow me to remind the Honourable Chamber that the UN Secretary-General presented his report pursuant to the UN Security Council Resolution number 808 to adopt the Statute of this Tribunal. On that occasion, the Secretary-General clearly emphasised that the principle of legality requires from an international Tribunal to apply the rules of international humanitarian law which had unequivocally become an integral part of international customary law. In terms of the Tribunal's subject matter jurisdiction, there's no dispute that the Geneva Conventions, The Hague Conventions, the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, the Statute of the International Military Court in Nuremberg, as well as the Resolutions of the International Law Commission from 1950, are its sources of law. Any other application of law or precedents beyond the aforementioned legal sources are always partially disputable and the Trial Chamber should necessarily provide a reasonable legal explanation for the application of certain legal institutes unknown to the aforementioned generally adopted international humanitarian law. In this case, the Defence is justifiably concerned about the incriminations that the Prosecutor imputes to the accused which point to the legal construct of expanded JCE. This is because there's no single provision in this Tribunal's Statute or in the aforementioned indisputable sources of international humanitarian law where the legal institute of joint criminal enterprise is mentioned. We have already heard counter- arguments according to which JCE is not even a separate crime but, rather, a form of criminal responsibility or command responsibility, which arises from the provisions of Article 7/1 and 7/3 of the Statute of this Tribunal. The Defence categorically refuses to accept this legal explanation and there will be legal arguments to corroborate the position of the Defence in this respect. Individual criminal responsibility of a natural person for crimes prosecuted according to international law has been unequivocally applied in the case law of ad hoc international tribunals. This Tribunal has established five types of criminal responsibility. Two principle ones, direct perpetration, on the one hand, and planning of a crime on the other. And three accessory ones: Aiding, abetting and any other form of action which has contributed to the planning or commission of a crime. The theory of command responsibility which arises under the Anglo-Saxon common law doctrine of vicarious liability is founded in the provision 7/3 of the Statute. The Appeals Chamber in Tadic case established by way of interpretation, per analogiam iuris, the construction of JCE as an alleged form of legal responsibility. In that, one should bear in mind that doctrine of vicarious liability originates from the Middle Ages as a responsibility of the superior for the damages inflicted upon third persons by their subordinates pursuant to the maxim respondeat superior. In Delalic case, the Trial Chamber established the following elements which constitute the term "indirect command responsibility" according to the standard comments of the legal profession as follows: Functional, dealing with the superior's position and a hierarchical relationship with his subordinates; cognitive, the superior's awareness that a subordinate is in the process of preparing to commit a crime or a crime has already been committed; and operational, a failure on the part of the superior to take the necessary and reasonable actions to prevent crimes or punish the perpetrators thereof. This standard of fact and law has imposed a heavy burden on the Prosecutor to prove his case. Hence, the Prosecutor has opted for an easier route, albeit a problematic one, from the legal point of view from the standard of fact and law in terms of joint criminal enterprise. As early as 2000, it was noticed that 81 per cent of all indictments -- indictments presented before this Tribunal were based on the JCE construct. Why was that? By applying this construct, the Prosecutor doesn't have to prove the cognitive and functional elements from Delalic indication, whereas the subjective element of the crime as a form of guilt, the so-called dolus eventualis, or an evil intent, is formulated so as to imply that the awareness of a possible commission of a crime encompasses also collateral crimes that the superior didn't have any knowledge of but, allegedly, he could have foreseen them due to the nature of a criminal plan or objective. In Tadic case, the Trial Chamber was not able to establish that the accused had participated in the killings of five Muslim civilians in the village of Jaksici, near Prijedor, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The killings had been committed by Serbian paramilitary troops engaged in the process of ethnic cleansing. Deciding on the Prosecutor's appeal on the part of the first instant Chamber's decision exculpating the accused from that charge, the Appeals Chamber reached a lucid decision and invented a systematic model of individual responsibility quite legally unfounded, from the Defence's point of view, and the Chamber based that model on the provision of Article 7 of the Statute. To arrive at its decision the Appeals Chamber had carried out an analysis of the jurisprudence of national courts and international tribunals after World War II with a view to establishing that postulate of indisputable element of the international humanitarian law which had been laid down by the UN Secretary-General in the previously quoted 1993 report. Likewise, the Appeals Chamber had established that the term "joint criminal enterprise" is entrenched in a minimum of two international treaties; the international convention for the suppression of terrorist bombings, dated 1997, and the 1998 Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court. Nota bene, Your Honours, both of these legal documents were drafted after the incriminated acts had been allegedly committed by the accused in 1995. Also, the Appeals Chamber established that the doctrine in the implementation of a joint intention is entrenched in international laws of many states. In short, the Appeals Chamber has established that the case law existed and that consequently joint criminal enterprise as a form of responsibility has its firm foundation in humanitarian law. Contrary to the above, the Defence believes that this conclusion is certainly not conclusive. In the Tadic case, which is what the Appeals Chamber analysed, there's no evidence that the Trial Chamber based its judgement on that legal construct. JCE does mention a joint plan and proffers conjectures as to whether and what way the competent court had really taken into account bases from such indictments. But this is by no accounts efficient to establish that the theory of the JCE, tempore criminis, which means that it coexisted with the crimes imputed to the accused, was part of international law. There is only one national court judgement, Italian court in Dottavio in 1947, in which the court based the guilt of the accused on something similar to the concept of extended JCE. But that judgement is not, nor can it indeed be, an equivocal proof that JCE is entrenched in international customary law. Subsequent judgements in Vasiljevic, Kvocka, Furundzija, and other cases have established the institute and the term "JCE" in the Tribunal's jurisprudence. In that, particularly interesting is a decision in Ojdanic case. The Defence in that case launched an appeal challenging the Tribunal's jurisdiction, and the Trial Chamber in that case confirmed its own jurisdiction with regard to the interpretation of the forms of criminal responsibility allegedly according to the Statute of the Tribunal. The introduction of such judicial practices at the Tribunal could not go unnoticed among the professional public. Many commentators have observed, rather cynically, that the Judges of the Tribunal stand to reap multiple benefits from the application of the legal construct of JCE in cases which would have otherwise been very complex. The contribution of participants has to be established in much broader terms than if the postulates of legality were applied. There's no longer the need to establish the elements of guilt of just one member of JCE which would connect them with the transgressions of other JCE members, as is stated in Krstic case. However, not all Tribunals Chambers or at least not all members of all the Chambers have been unanimous in their way of thinking and in adopting the legal novelty which was JCE. In the Stakic, for example, the Trial Chamber states that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am asked to convey the message to you that you're speaking too quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I was afraid of it, Your Honour, and I will try to do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And just for me also to understand the argument raised, you effectively are asking this Trial Chamber not to follow the case law of this Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and to say that we have no jurisdiction if it is about joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Then if you would please continue at such a pace that transcribers and interpreters can follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour. [Interpretation] In Stakic case, for example, the Trial Chamber states that a restricted interpretation of the provisions of the Statute based on national interpretative methods would be more desirable for those provisions of the Statute which deal with perpetration. This would avoid a misleading impression that a new crime not foreseen in the Statute of this Tribunal has been introduced through the back door. That's paragraph 441. The legal term of a joint criminal enterprise is much too broad a form of co-perpetration, and actually, it constitutes a legal fiction which makes it possible for a person to be prosecuted and convicted for crimes committed by another person even if the former had no intention of contributing to the latter person's crime and possibly had not even been aware of the latter person's actions. Legal experts and writers have published a lot of papers about this topic. I would like to point the Trial Chamber to the work of Professor Kai Ambos, chair of criminal law at Goettingen University, as well as Professor Ciara Damgaard from Copenhagen University, as well as a former chief judge for the Egyptian Ministry of Justice, Dr. Mohamed Elewa Badar, who is the author of an ironical translation for the acronym JCE in English and he says that it stands for "just convict everyone." Likewise, I would like to remind you of the Statute of the ICC and its provisions. That Statute was passed at the so-called Rome Conference with a view of having that UN court and the international criminal system confirm the principles and rules that will ensure highest standards of justice. And these rules would have been -- rules would have been better served had they been included in the Statute themselves rather than left to the courts exercising their discretion. It is precisely for that reason that the Rome Statute, in view of the number of participants involved within it was being passed, and in view of the three years that it took, it is considered to be the codification of customary international law and crimes committed at an international level. This process is also considered to be and described as the factual consolidation of the principles of national criminal jurisdictions at an international level. The authors of the Statute did not intend to create new legal rules or create a new form of criminal liability. Philippe Kirsch, the first president of the ICC, established that it was not the task of the Statute to create new substantive law but, rather, to include those crimes that have already been recognised and prohibited on the basis of existing international law. The intentional non-conclusion of the institute of joint criminal enterprise in the Rome Statute is an indicative fact on the basis of which it may be concluded, with full justification, that joint criminal enterprise should not be considered part of customary international law. The principle of legality is based on the following premises. The prohibition of retroactive punishment by law, nullum crimen sine lege praevia; the prohibition of analogy, nullum crimen sine lege stricta; the requirement that written legislation must exist, nullum crimen sine lege scripta; the requirement that law must be defined exactly, nullum crimen sine lege certa; and the principle that there shall be no punishment without law, nulla poena sine lege. In addition to the undisputed acceptability of the principle of legality in national criminal systems of contemporary legal orders, the obligation to observe that principle is prescribed in fundamental documents of international law governing human rights; that is to say, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Article 15; the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Articles 11 and 2; the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms of the Council of Europe, Article 7. In the case of S.W. against the United Kingdom, and C.R. v. the United Kingdom, the European Court, as far as back as 1995, explicitly stated that these provisions on observing the principles of legality cannot be derogated even in a case of war or another emergency. In the Statute of the Tribunal there is no explicit provision involving the principle of legality but the report of the Secretary-General of the UN refers to it when stating that the application of the principle nullum crimen sine lege makes it incumbent upon the Tribunal to apply rules of international humanitarian that have quite certainly, beyond any doubt, become part of customary law. Otherwise there would be a problem. Namely, that only some states, rather than all states, having to abide by certain convention. For example, the United States of America never accepted the Rome Statute and therefore, in theory, by strict application of international covenants, they wouldn't have to respect the principle of legality which, of course, from a legal and civilisational point of view, would be a completely absurd situation. Bearing in mind the criteria of accessibility and foreseeability, it is not sufficient for a court to establish only the objective capability of an accused person to recognise a repressive or prohibitive norm, but also the subjective capacity of a specific accused person to anticipate and recognise his or her own criminal liability that would be the consequence of a violation of such a norm. The objective understanding of foreseeability in terms of extended joint criminal enterprise, it gets dangerously close to objective responsibility which seriously brings into question the principle of liability that is explicitly accepted by the Tribunal itself. It is clear that internal law that was in force in the territory of the former SFRY, tempore criminis, nevertheless has to be taken into account and special attention has to be devoted to it in view of this subjective element. Therefore, it is surprising that the Chambers of the Tribunal so far have not expressed any great interest in studying national law and jurisprudence. It is correct that neither the Statute nor the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal do not refer to national law except in terms of sentencing, and only partially at that. But it is equally true that in terms of accessible and foreseeability, one should investigate at least the basic legal institutes that existed in the territory of the former SFRY, tempore criminis. In our view -- [In English] I'm still too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to repeat the message. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm constantly looking at the clock and I'm trying to finish my presentation up in the time, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but not at the expense of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry, once again, to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] The Defence is pointing out the dissenting view of Judge Cassese in the Erdemovic case; namely, that is necessary to analyse the law of states from the countries that the accused persons come from. That is to say, that the citizen of any one of these states, Croatia included, was duty-bound to be familiar with criminal law in the territory of that state and therefore base one's expectations on that. Judge Cassese, in paragraph 49, says that it would be proper and reasonable to look at the national legislation of the accused rather than moral considerations or practical principles, because the general rule of in dubio pro reo also works in favour of that. There is no doubt that sometimes it is truly difficult to see what customary law is because it comes into being as unwritten law. It is only when it is legally established that an action was carried out because it was a legal obligation, opinio juris; that is, it is only then that customary law is established. Whoever claims that there is a rule of customary law has to prove constant, general, and consistent practice to that effect. Therefore, what has to be referred to is the largest possible number of examples from jurisprudence -- from practice, from case law, in which subjects of international law acted in accordance with a particular rule. Opinio juris can only be established on that basis as a prerequisite for a rule of customary law to come into being. In seems that in relation to the institute of joint criminal enterprise, opinio juris is simply not there. At least it would not fall under the phrase of "beyond any reasonable doubt." It is part of customary law. The Defence claims that the Prosecutor did not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that opinio juris exists in view of the doctrine of joint criminal enterprise, notably category 3. Actually the Prosecutor didn't deal with this at all. And it seems as if they believe that -- that it is a presumption such as presumptio juris et de jure. However, I would like to recall views to the contrary, views that are contrary to the views of the Tadic Trial Chamber. The Pre-Trial Chamber of the Special Court for Cambodia, ECCC, in case number 002/19-09-2007, in their decision reached on 20th May this year, concludes that, I quote: "The principle of legality requires that the ECCC should refrain from relying on extended joint criminal enterprise in their activities." This Chamber did not find any support for the existence of joint criminal enterprise category 3, tempore criminis, in -- in customary international law, and the Tadic Chamber referred to that specifically. The same view is held by the Pre-Trial Chamber of the ICC, the International Criminal Court, in the case of Lubanga. And they state that they particularly disassociate themselves from the excessively subjective concept of JCE. The same court, in the Katanga case, on the basis of a decision reached by the Appeals Chamber, rejects this form of responsibility, stating that it is not part of customary international law. The same position was articulated in the Bemba case as well. May I remind you that may not all the Judges in this Tribunal share the views of the Tadic Trial Chamber. For example, Judge Per-Johan Lindholm in the Simic case, disassociates himself from the concept of the doctrine of joint criminal enterprise in that case, but also in general terms. I would particularly like to point out the position of a former Judge of this Tribunal, Wolfgang Schomburg, who, in an article he has published on 3rd of June, this year, in the blog Cambodia Tribunal Monitor, says that the decision in the Tadic case regarding the institute of extended joint criminal enterprise gave rise to criticism in professional circles because of the potential excessive application. And that, therefore, this Tribunal has to take this criticism seriously so that the theory of joint criminal enterprise would not grow into guilt by association. Judge Schomburg says that customary international law and the principle of legality are like cat and dog. On the one hand, there is an wish to sanction something; and, on the other hand, there is the dicta that new criminal law should not be established retroactively. Judge Schomburg believes that the decision of the Pre-Trial Chamber of the Special Court for Cambodia is amazing in its meticulous analysis of the decisions of courts after the Second World War and that the said decision is a more-than-welcome development after years of dangerous confusion. And the reference being made is to the application of the doctrine of extended joint criminal enterprise. The decision of the Trial Chamber in the Brdjanin case states that the Prosecutor, if wishing to prove joint criminal enterprise, must identify the physical perpetrator of the crime involved and prove that there was agreement between accused and the direct perpetrator on the perpetration of a specific crime. The Chamber refused to apply the doctrine of joint criminal enterprise, thereby making a significant turnaround in view of the case law of the Tribunal up until then. Obviously when decisions were being made by different Chambers of the Tribunal, there were differences in understanding legal institutes, and this division is also due to the differences between common law and civil law systems. For example, in the Stakic case, the Chamber decided to exchange the doctrine of joint criminal enterprise with the institute of co-perpetration. His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen indicated that problem in his dissenting opinion in the appeals case of Gacumbitsi, where he brings into question the existence of opinio juris because some states accept the theory of joint criminal enterprise, whereas others accept and apply the theory of co-perpetration. The Defence therefore believes that when the theory of extended joint criminal enterprise was introduced, what was brought into question was acting outside international law and the mandate entrusted to the Tribunal by the Security Council of the UN. And finally, I would like to say the following. I believe that it very important to point out the unacceptable procedure on the part of the Prosecutor with regard to the members of the JCE, which the Prosecutor describes as people who have died in the meantime; Dr. Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak, Janko Bobetko, Zvonimir Cervenko. One would seriously question the moral and legal foundation for including persons no longer living among the participants of a joint criminal enterprise and even labelling them as co-perpetrators. Without valid arguments and in view of the fact that the aforementioned persons are not in a position to defend themselves from such qualifications, the Prosecutor has presumed their criminal responsibility for the same acts that the accused have been charged with in the indictment issued ex post facto. The same is true of other individuals. Although alive, they have never been summoned as witnesses or in -- in any other capacities -- capacity. Even Jarnjak, minister of the interior, tempore criminis; Mirko Norac, commander of Gospic Military District; Milenko Crnjac, commander of Karlovac Military District; Rahim Ademi, commander of Military District North and the accused Gotovina's second in command. Or, some of them have been summoned as witnesses but were never confronted with incriminations and arguments based on evidence according to which they too were members of JCE, or that they were used as JCE tools or instruments. Thus, they were never given a fair chance to stand up in their defence. I'm referring to witnesses Radic, Lausic and Moric. The most questionable, however, is the category of persons, JCE members, whom the Prosecutor describes as different officers and officials, members of the Republic of Croatia government and political officials at all levels, including those in municipal and local organisations, various leaders and members of the HDZ, the Croatian Army, the special police, the civilian police, and other intelligence and security services in the Republic of Croatia, and other known and unknown individuals. The Prosecutor labels certain categories of persons as co-perpetrators and/or members of JCE and/or JCE instruments in a way which is simply intolerable and inadmissible from the legal standpoint. In that, these persons do not have any means at stating their case about the presumed guilt imputed to them by the Prosecutor. This procedure is clearly contrary to the presumption of innocence. Let me remind you of the Stakic case decision which says, and I quote: "There is not enough evidence in this case to prove that a genocidal campaign was being planned at a higher level. The persons belonging to the vertical hierarchical structure are all deceased, hence, the evidence cannot be adduced." This standpoint is of particular significance in a situation where the existence of a discriminatory intent as a form of guilt has to be proven both for a crime of genocide as well as a crime of persecution, which is what our client has been charged with. In other words, dolus specialis has to be established and, needless to say, this is particularly difficult to prove in cases of dead JCE members or co-perpetrators. In conclusion, the Defence states the following. Joint criminal enterprise never existed as an element of the -- of international customary law, tempore criminis, as alleged in the indictment. And I'm referring to category 3. JCE is contrary to the principle of guilt as one of the fundamental principles of modern criminal law. The application of JCE is a dangerous way to expand the notion of mens rea and brings this absolutely close to guilt by association, especially in view of the extended form of JCE. The principle of presumption of innocence has been violated by the application of a conclusion about the existence of an intention on the part of the accused based on objective circumstances as stipulated by the doctrine of extended JCE. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal, as well as the jurisprudence of courts and tribunals which have operated after World War II, is neither unanimous nor consistent in terms of the JCE content theory, which is contrary to the principle of justice and fairness before a court of law and thus does not constitute a -- an opinio juris. The application of the JCE doctrine, across the board, on all political and military structures in a state administration as well as on other known and unknown individuals constitutes a violation of the principle of [indiscernible] and precision of charges which threatens the very purpose of the Tribunal's establishment and existence, and increases the risk arising from an even more extensive use of the JCE theory by national courts and prosecutors in national jurisdictions. All this may have an adverse effect in the process of reaffirming the position of modern criminal law and administration of justice. Your Honours, finally, the Defence suggests that the Trial Chamber did one step ahead to evaluate the arguments about not accepting the theory of JCE which clearly exist in modern legal science and were proffered by various authors. They're clearly present in the way the Judges of this Tribunal think. They are clearly evident in the decisions of various courts and Tribunals after the Second World War and to -- to the application of the doctrine of JCE and to go back to the principles of the liability that exists in criminal law, which is co-perpetration, aiding, abetting. But, in that case, some other requirements of adducing evidence and proving guilt will apply, different from those applied to the doctrine of the JCE in its extended form. I would like to thank you, Your Honour, for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. This concludes today's session. Tomorrow we'll hear any rebuttal argument from the Prosecution. I appreciate that the parties did their utmost best to stay within the time-limits which leaves us a bit more time perhaps tomorrow. Not to say that we -- that we would use the whole of the morning, that is, three sessions, but it with not be dramatic if the parties, and one hour scheduled for the Prosecution and one hour for the Defence teams, would take a little bit more than that one hour. I suggest that the Prosecution takes the session until the first break tomorrow morning, and that the Defence then will take the second session. Of course, it depends a bit, Mr. Tieger, if would you take the full one hour and a half, I know what is going to happen. So if you would apply some self-limitation and seek compensation perhaps for not having had an opportunity to -- to make final conclusions after Ms. Mahindaratne had spoken, then we could avoid perhaps that we would need a third session and we would perhaps finish the second session also in, let's say, 75 minutes. We adjourn, and we will resume tomorrow, the 1st of September, at 9.00, in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of September, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
